## 17.6 Semi-Liquid Vehicles and the Redemption Game

### 17.6.1 Desk framing: the failure mode moved from defaults to redemptions

Retail money became the marginal private-credit dollar. Semi-liquid vehicles (perpetual non-traded BDCs and interval funds) held about \$425 billion gross and \$241 billion net by the Fed's May 2026 count, about one-fifth of private credit's net AUM, and in the first quarter of 2026 accepted redemptions exceeded inflows for the first time (Fed *Financial Stability Report*, May 8, 2026). Non-traded BDCs hold about 0.2% of assets in short-term liquid instruments, with debt to equity of 0.90 (George and Shin, October 14, 2026). Their liquidity is not cash. It is bank lines, loan repayments and a sleeve of syndicated loans held to be sold.

That changes what can go wrong. A drawdown fund with ten-year locked capital fails, if it fails, through defaults. A semi-liquid fund that promises quarterly repurchases at NAV can fail through *redemptions* while its loans perform, because the NAV it pays out is smoothed and everyone knows it. The IMF put the mechanism precisely: slow-moving valuations create a first-mover advantage, and discretionary gating "may erode investor confidence across the broader industry" (IMF *Global Financial Stability Report*, April 2026, ch. 1).

Theo recognizes the problem instantly, which is a strange feeling for a man three weeks into a quant desk. A fund facing a redemption queue is a borrower facing a maturity wall, and his thirteen-week cash flow model, still on the USB stick, needs only three row renames: "revolver availability" becomes undrawn lines, "asset sales" becomes the syndicated sleeve, and "maturities" becomes the redemption cap. The model that refuses to die has found its next body: a liquidity runway measured in quarters.

### 17.6.2 Derivation: a run with a pro-rata cap

**Notation.** NAV per share is $N$ (smoothed); the true value per share is $N(1-m)$, with $m$ the markdown of §17.3. The quarterly cap is $c$ (typically 5% of shares). The request fraction is $a_t$, which we deliberately do not call $q$, a letter this book reserves for dealer inventory. The fill fraction is $f_t=\min(1,c/a_t)$, and the share of the fund actually redeemed is $p_t=f_ta_t=\min(a_t,c)$.

**The transfer.** With $S$ shares outstanding, redeemers receive $N$ per share on $p_tS$ shares and the stayers own what is left. Post-redemption true value per remaining share is

$$
N^{\text{true}}_{\text{stay}}=\frac{N(1-m)S-N\,p_tS}{S(1-p_t)}=N\cdot\frac{(1-m)-p_t}{1-p_t}.
$$

Compare it with the no-run value $N(1-m)$:

$$
N^{\text{true}}_{\text{stay}}<N(1-m)
\iff (1-m)-p_t<(1-m)(1-p_t)
\iff p_t\,m>0 .
$$

So stayers lose whenever anyone redeems and $m>0$. The total transfer is exactly $p_tSNm$, the redeemed shares times the overpayment per share, and it lands on the $(1-p_t)S$ shares that stayed.

**The game.** An investor who requests gets $N$ on a fraction $f_t$ of her shares and $N^{\text{true}}_{\text{stay}}$ on the rest; one who does not gets $N^{\text{true}}_{\text{stay}}$ on everything. Since $N>N(1-m)>N^{\text{true}}_{\text{stay}}$ when $m>0$, requesting pays $f_t\big(N-N^{\text{true}}_{\text{stay}}\big)>0$ more, for any $f_t>0$. **Requesting is a dominant strategy as soon as $m>0$ is believed**, net of whatever small early-repurchase fee or tax friction applies. The cap does not remove the first-mover advantage; it rations it. If everyone requests, $a_t=1$, $f_t=c$, and the fund pays out $c$ per quarter: a 5% cap turns a run into a twenty-quarter queue.

Why, then, do request fractions sit at 6% or 17% rather than 100%? Because $m$ is not common knowledge. Most holders came through an advisor, few read the 10-Q, and many do not know a listed sibling exists. The request fraction $a_t$ is therefore a *belief* variable: the share of holders who are both attentive and persuaded that $m>0$. It jumps when a public signal coordinates beliefs, which is why a listed sibling printing 0.86 of book, or a merger at NAV-for-NAV, moves the non-traded fund's queue.

**Queue dynamics.** Unfilled tender requests usually lapse and must be resubmitted, and in practice most are, which behaves like a rolling backlog $\mathcal{B}_t$. With new requests arriving as a fraction $a^{\text{new}}_t$ of non-queued shares, demand is $\mathcal{B}_t+a^{\text{new}}_t(S_t-\mathcal{B}_t)$, payouts are $\min(\text{demand},cS_t)$, the backlog carries the rest, and $S_{t+1}=S_t-\text{payout}$. Fill rates fall quarter after quarter even if new requests are steady, and that falling fill is itself a public signal that feeds the next quarter's $a^{\text{new}}$.

**Liquidity runway.** In quarters, for a vehicle with NAV normalized to one,

$$
\mathcal{T}=\frac{\text{Cash}+\text{Undrawn lines}+\text{Sleeve}\times(1-h)}{c\cdot\text{NAV}+\text{Unfunded draws}+\text{Debt maturities}-\text{Repayments}},
$$

where $h$ is the haircut on the syndicated sleeve under stress and every flow in the denominator is per quarter. If the denominator is zero or negative, the runway is unbounded. The IMF's calibration target is 9–11 quarters of 5% redemptions under mild stress and 5–7 under a moderate shock. The repayment term links this section to §17.4: repayments *are* the private book's exit hazards, $\kappa^{(B)}+\kappa^{(P)}$, and those fall in a tight-loan regime, exactly when redemptions rise. Two error-prone spots deserve emphasis. First, $h$ is reflexive: when several funds sell their sleeves at once, the sale *is* the spillover into public loan prices, and the haircut rises because of the selling it is meant to measure. Second, the fund can change $c$. OBDC II's move from tenders to return-of-capital distributions changed the payout rule, and with it the game.

> **Poker Table.** Ines draws the redemption queue as a hand. "Twenty players, one pot, and the dealer will only pay five percent of the pot per round, pro rata among whoever stands up. Everyone can see a card face down in the middle; it's the true NAV. Nobody can turn it over, but there's a mirror across the room, the listed sibling's price, and it says the card is worse than the dealer claims. The first players to believe the mirror stand up first and get paid at the dealer's number. Everyone else is subsidizing them. You don't win this hand by being right about the card. You win by being early about the mirror." Then she replays it through markouts: in the first quarter of 2026, the investors who requested in January were filled at a NAV that later quarters marked down.

### Case Study: The Redemption Quarters of 2026

**Q1 2026.** Investors sought about \$13 billion from "over a dozen funds," and with quarterly caps around 5% of net assets "more than \$4.6 billion of investor capital" was trapped behind withdrawal limits (Bloomberg Law, March 26, 2026). Barings capped a private credit fund at 5% after requests reported at 11.3% of shares, and Moody's reportedly moved its outlook on a large Blue Owl non-traded BDC to negative (press reports, early April 2026; not independently verified for this edition). The Fed's May report recorded that accepted redemptions exceeded inflows for the first time and that several funds received requests "much larger than 5 percent of NAV."

**Q2 2026.** Apollo Debt Solutions, a \$26 billion fund, saw requests reach "16.8%, equivalent to \$2.4 billion" and capped them at 5% of shares, "the standard limit for such vehicles"; Blue Owl's two non-traded BDCs received April exit requests of "roughly 20% and 40%"; Blackstone's \$79 billion BCRED received repurchase requests "amounting to 10% of shares outstanding" for the quarter to June 30; and Morgan Stanley's North Haven Private Income Fund had limited repurchases to 5% in March (InvestmentNews, June 23, 2026).

**The model mapping.** At $a=0.168$ and $c=0.05$ the fill is $0.05/0.168\approx30\%$. With an illustrative markdown of $m=5\%$, each quarter's redemptions transfer $p\,m=0.25\%$ of NAV from stayers to redeemers, and the stayers' true value per share falls from $0.950$ to $0.947$ of NAV. That is small per quarter and corrosive over five, which is why the funds' choices matter more than the arithmetic. They can sell the sleeve, which pushes public loan prices down; draw the bank line, which in 2022 cost an extra 1.1 points; or change the rules, as OBDC II did when it replaced tenders with return-of-capital distributions funded by the \$1.4 billion sale.

**The desk signal.** The request percentage per fund is a public, dated, numeric series: it appears in 8-Ks, tender-offer filings (Schedule TO) and fund letters within days of each quarter's deadline. It leads listed-BDC equity and BDC bond spreads, because it is the most direct measure of how many holders believe $m>0$. Build the `redemptions` table before anything else in this chapter; it is the cheapest data with the highest signal-to-noise.

> **Trend Watch.** *The listed discount and the redemption queue, November 2025 to September 2026.* November 5–19, 2025: the OBDC/OBDC II NAV-for-NAV merger is announced and terminated within fourteen days (Blue Owl releases). February 18, 2026: OBDC repurchases stock at a reported 86% of book (check against the OBDC Q4 release); OBDC II replaces tender offers with return-of-capital distributions (Blue Owl releases). March 26, 2026: about \$13 billion of first-quarter requests, more than \$4.6 billion trapped (Bloomberg Law). End of March 2026: the median listed BDC is reported at about 0.74 times forward NAV, the widest since 2020 (Reuters/LSEG; not independently verified). April 14, 2026: the IMF estimates non-traded BDCs can meet 5% quarterly redemptions for 9–11 quarters under mild stress and 5–7 under a moderate shock. April 16, 2026: listed BDCs at "nearly a 20% discount," some large names "approaching a 50% discount" (Octus). May 8, 2026: the Fed FSR reports that, for perpetual BDCs, accepted redemptions exceeded inflows in Q1 2026, the first time since those vehicles were created. June 23, 2026: a \$26 billion fund at 16.8% requests and a \$79 billion fund at 10% (InvestmentNews). **What it means for the desk:** the dispersion of listed discounts, not their mean, is the tradable signal (§17.9), and the redemption series is its leading indicator.

The runway check is a non-traded BDC with 0.2% cash, an undrawn line of 10% of NAV and a 10% syndicated sleeve haircut by 10%, paying 5% redemptions and 2% of NAV a quarter in unfunded draws *(illustrative)*. With no repayments it lasts under three quarters; with repayments of 3% of NAV a quarter it lasts 4.8, just under the IMF's moderate-shock range. Everything turns on the repayment rate, and the repayment rate is the hazard model of §17.4.

> **Ways This Blows Up.** (1) *Treating the sleeve as cash.* The haircut is a function of how many other funds are selling the same loans that week. (2) *Assuming the rules are fixed.* Boards can suspend tenders, switch to return-of-capital distributions, or (in some structures) raise the cap; each changes the game mid-hand. (3) *Ignoring the bank.* A borrowing-base haircut on PIK or non-accrual loans shrinks the undrawn line exactly when the queue lengthens, which is the question Theo asked in the cold open. (4) *Reading low requests as health.* A falling $a_t$ after a gate may mean investors gave up, not that they were reassured; check whether the backlog was resubmitted.

## 17.7 The Plumbing That Turns Marks into Prices

### 17.7.1 Desk framing: a 2022 prediction, scored in 2026

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Man_Quantitative_Credit_Alpha_Early_Mover_2022 p.41:* "While loans and other private credit instruments are obviously problematic from a data availability perspective at present, we believe that the momentum of quant activity in other areas of the fixed income markets will drive innovation and transparency in these historically opaque areas. Already both Refinitiv and IHS Markit are providing daily pricing on 6,500 loan facilities."
>
> **Annotation.** Four years later the prediction scores well on infrastructure and poorly on causation. Private credit did acquire identifiers, daily estimated values, a secondary desk, a CDS index with private-credit names in it and an official statistics line, all between 2025 and 2026. But the driver was not quant activity spilling over from public bonds. It was the wealth channel: managers competing for retail and 401(k) money needed something that looked like a daily price, and stressed redemption queues made the absence of one expensive. The desk's departure from Man's framing is practical. The new data are not prices in the sense of Chapter 19's TRACE prints; most of them are *marks published more often*. The smoothing kernel of §17.2 still applies, with shorter lags.

Mags has her own version. "Back in my day, distressed was the private market. You called three desks, got a 32–34 market on five million, and the bid evaporated if you said the word 'size.'" Moyer's description of the old distressed market is still the best one: "Liquidity, of course, is a matter of degree" (Moyer_Distressed_Debt_Analysis p.313). Then the grudging respect: "A firm bid that a manager is contractually obliged to honor every day? We'd have killed for that. Check who's on the other side of it."

### 17.7.2 Five price sources, and what each one actually measures

1. **Listed BDC equity and bonds.** True market prices, set by people who can lose money, on a wrapper that includes fees and leverage. §17.3 inverts them.
2. **Daily estimated values from managers.** Apollo extended daily pricing from its investment-grade products (July 1, 2026) to direct lending, asset-backed finance, multi-credit and opportunistic vehicles on October 1, 2026, with asset-level pricing from October 30, 2026. The release is careful to call it an internal estimated fair value, "not a market-clearing price" (Apollo release, October 1, 2026). A daily mark is still a mark. It stair-steps on smaller stairs.
3. **Identifiers and a secondary market.** ICE's private credit service had issued more than 5,000 ICE IDs by March 2026, and Apollo reported more than \$30 billion of secondary trading since 2024 (same release). Identifiers matter more than they sound: they are the join key that turns fifty BDC schedules of investments into one panel, which is what the cross-holder dispersion of §17.3 needs.
4. **A contractual bid.** The SPDR SSGA IG Public & Private Credit ETF (PRIV) launched in February 2025 with a 10–35% private-credit policy. At October 15, 2026 it held \$802.8 million in 363 positions, about 22.1% sourced from Apollo, and Apollo must post daily firm, executable bids on those assets and buy them back at those bids within stress-redemption limits (State Street fund page). The smoothing problem becomes a counterparty problem: the ETF's private sleeve is worth what Apollo's bid is worth, up to the facility's limits.
5. **Credit derivatives.** S&P Dow Jones Indices announced a CDX Financials index in early 2026, reported to contain 25 North American financial names including BDCs and private-credit managers, with trading from April 2026 (S&P DJI announcement, February 25, 2026; constituents and weights not verified for this edition). It is the first $\mathbb{Q}$-measure instrument with private credit inside it, and §17.9 explains why it is a worse hedge than it looks.

> **Trend Watch.** *From "no price" to five price sources, 2022–2026.* 2022: Man notes daily vendor pricing on 6,500 syndicated loan facilities and calls private credit "problematic from a data availability perspective" (Man p.41). February 2025: PRIV launches with a manager's firm bid on its private sleeve (State Street). March 2026: ICE passes 5,000 private-credit identifiers (Apollo release). April 2026: CDX Financials begins trading, reportedly with BDCs among its names (S&P DJI; details unverified). July 1 and October 1, 2026: Apollo daily pricing reaches investment-grade and then all credit vehicles; asset-level from October 30 (Apollo). October 16, 2026: private credit enters the Fed's Z.1 with holder-level series (Brinkman et al.). **What it means for the desk:** for the first time there are enough *public* observations of *private* marks to estimate the kernel, the gap and the lead–lag on live data rather than on CDLI back-fills. Wire each source into Appendix B's data atlas with its own measurement label: price, mark, bid or spread.

## 17.8 Systematic Approaches to Private Credit

### 17.8.1 Desk framing: four marks a year and a lot of footnotes

What can "systematic" mean for an asset that reports four times a year? Not high-frequency anything. It means a **look-through security master** built from BDC schedules of investments (every facility, every quarter, with cost, fair value, spread, lien and PIK flags) plus a set of slow, fundamental features computed on it. The corpus is research-grade: Davydiuk, Marchuk and Rosen used BDC schedule-of-investment data to show that BDC capital substitutes for bank credit after regulatory and lender-specific supply shocks ("Direct Lenders in the U.S. Middle Market," *Journal of Financial Economics* 162, 2024). Chapter 25's parser builds the table; this section says what to compute on it.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Bohn_Stein_Active_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.235 (fn. 11):* "it would be unusual in the private credit risk setting to have more than 10 year-end financial statements and quarterly financial statements."
>
> **Annotation.** Bohn and Stein are describing borrower-level data for private-firm default models, and the warning transfers directly to vehicle-level work: forty quarterly NAVs is a long history for a BDC, and many semi-liquid funds have fewer than twenty. Every estimate in this chapter (the kernel, the lead–lag, the hazard loadings) is a small-sample estimate, so the 2026 desk departs from single-vehicle modeling altogether. It pools across vehicles that hold the same loans, as Couts, Gonçalves and Rossi recommend; it uses purged, embargoed cross-validation with quarterly blocks (Chapter 7); and it reports intervals. The breadth of a private-credit strategy comes from the cross-section of vehicles and facilities, not from the time series of any one of them.

### 17.8.2 The features worth computing

- **Sector and AI exposure.** About one-fifth of direct-lending loans are to software companies, and software can exceed half of NAV in some levered vehicles (IMF GFSR, April 2026). Public markets repriced first: syndicated loan spreads widened "reflecting a high concentration of leveraged loan borrowers in the software industry" before private-credit new-loan spreads "ticked up" (Fed FSR, May 2026). A per-vehicle software loading is a sector factor in Chapter 9's framework.
- **Diversification.** BDCs with more than 200 borrowers averaged a 9.5% return on equity in 2025, against 6.1% for those with fewer than 100 (Cliffwater data via BlackRock *Private Credit Primer*, January 2026). Scale is a factor, not a footnote.
- **Hidden default.** PIK interest was 7.3% of CDLI income in 2025 (Cliffwater, March 31, 2026). Of investments paying PIK at the end of 2025, 58.3% carried "bad PIK," meaning PIK amended in after closing rather than agreed at origination (Lincoln International data via BlackRock's *Credit Currents* chartbook, 1H2026). Kaz asks whether that means there is a good PIK. There is: a PIK toggle priced into the original deal is a contract term. A PIK amended in after closing is a borrower who could not pay cash and a lender who preferred not to call it a default. Theo's "but what does the amendment say?" is, here, the entire feature.
- **Mark quality.** Stale-mark share (§17.3), cross-holder dispersion (§17.3) and the gap series $g_t$.
- **Net-of-fee reality.** Private debt funds' net-of-fee abnormal returns are statistically insignificant; gross alpha is positive, and so is alpha against a debt-only benchmark, which reflects embedded equity risk (Erel, Flanagan and Weisbach, NBER w32278, 2024). IDO or it didn't happen: strip leveraged-loan beta, rates and the equity-like tail before calling anything alpha.
- **Collateral uniqueness.** The unit-sum constraint of §17.2 fails when the collateral was never there. First Brands (Chapter 11, September 2025), Tricolor and the UK lender Market Financial Solutions were all accompanied by allegations that receivables or loans had been pledged to more than one lender (press and court reports; amounts not verified for this edition). No smoothing kernel catches that. A UCC lien-overlap check and a flag for receivables bought off-platform do.

### 17.8.3 Derivation: what the public data already knows about the next marks

The chapter's main engine combines §17.2 and §17.3. Under the smoothing model, the true value change through quarter $t$ is $\beta\sum_{s\le t}F_s$ (ignoring the idiosyncratic part, which has mean zero), and the marks through $t$ have recognized $\beta\sum_{s\le t}F_s\sum_{k=0}^{t-s}\theta_k$ of it. The difference is the **pending mark**:

$$
\Pi_t=\beta\sum_{s\le t}F_s\Big(1-\sum_{k=0}^{t-s}\theta_k\Big)=\beta\sum_{j=0}^{K-1}\bar\Theta_{j+1}\,F_{t-j},
\qquad \bar\Theta_{j}\equiv\sum_{k=j}^{K}\theta_k ,
$$

using $j=t-s$ and the unit-sum constraint, so that $1-\sum_{k=0}^{j}\theta_k=\bar\Theta_{j+1}$. $\Pi_t$ is the sum of all future reported returns already implied by public factor returns, known at $t$. With $\theta=(0.5,0.3,0.2)$, $\Pi_t=\beta(0.5F_t+0.2F_{t-1})$. If the loan index fell 4% this quarter and was flat last quarter, a unit-beta book still has 2% of markdowns to come.

The **mark-gap signal** compares that mechanical catch-up with what the listed price implies:

$$
G_{i,t}=m_{i,t}-\max\!\big(0,-\Pi_{i,t}\big).
$$

When $G_{i,t}>0$, the price discounts more than the public data says the marks will fall: either the market knows something about this book beyond its beta (high software share, bad PIK, stale marks), or it is overreacting. The cross-sectional regression of $G$ on the §17.8.2 features separates the two, and the residual is the relative-value signal. When $G_{i,t}<0$, the price has not caught up with marks that are coming, which is the cleanest short in the book.

## 17.9 What a Public-Markets Quant Desk Can Arbitrage

You cannot buy the loans. You can trade every public instrument whose price is a function of private marks. The menu, with the signal from this chapter that drives each one:

| Trade | Instruments | Signal | Hedge | Main failure mode |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| BDC equity relative value | Long scaled, diversified, low-software, low-bad-PIK BDCs; short sub-scale ones | Residual of $G_{i,t}$ on features; stale-mark share; cross-holder dispersion | Leveraged-loan TRS, loan ETF or HY CDX for beta; equity index for the equity tail | Borrow cost and buyback squeezes on the short side |
| BDC capital structure | Unsecured notes vs equity (revolver senior to both) | Deleveraging, asset sales near par, bank line pricing and utilization | Ratio from a Merton-on-a-CLO map (Chapter 23) | Thin bond trading; a single buyer can take a whole new issue |
| Index vs basket | CDX Financials vs a BDC-only basket | BDC spread dispersion vs index | Ratio-weighted index protection | Few private-credit names in the index: small, unstable hedge ratio |
| Wrapper premium/discount | PRIV and future hybrid ETFs | Premium/discount vs firm-bid facility headroom | Public IG sleeve | Facility limits bind in stress; counterparty concentration |
| Event-driven | Mergers at NAV, tender-to-RoC conversions, listings, portfolio sales | Exchange-ratio math, request percentages | Sector basket | Adverse selection in sales "at fair value" |
| Gate-driven selling | Syndicated loans held in semi-liquid sleeves | Quarter-end queues, runway $\mathcal{T}$ | Loan index | Crowded, small, and quickly arbitraged |
| Takeout supply | CLO tranches, repricing-sensitive loans | $Q^{P\to B}$ from §17.4 | CLO AAA vs equity | Misread regime; dual-track noise |
| Insurer rotation | Public BBB/BB vs MM-CLO mezzanine | NAIC calendar, designation challenges | Duration-matched IG index | Regulatory delay; the rotation is pre-announced |

Two of these deserve a warning label.

> **Ways This Blows Up.** (1) *The index hedge that isn't.* CDX Financials is a broad financials index with only a handful of private-credit names, so its beta to a BDC basket is small and moves with bank and insurer news that has nothing to do with marks. Hedging a BDC bond book with it is hedging a cough with an umbrella. (2) *The sale at fair value.* Every portfolio sale at or near par is evidence about the loans that were sold, not the loans that were kept. Treat a "sale at 99.7% of par" as an upper bound on the remaining book's marks, never as a confirmation of them. (3) *Equity beta in disguise.* Listed BDC equity carries equity-market beta that rises in selloffs; a BDC relative-value book that is not hedged against the equity index will look like private-credit alpha until the first equity drawdown. (4) *Crowding the obvious.* By mid-2026 every desk had the redemption series. The edge moved to its *second derivative*, the change in fill rates and backlog, and to vehicles whose sibling relationships are less obvious than Blue Owl's.

## 17.10 Desk Debrief

Ines replays the cold-open hand. The desk bid the \$25mm of notes two points back of the screen and hedged half the risk with a short in the BDC's own equity, on the view that the seller knew about the redemption queue at a sibling-type vehicle and the equity would reprice before the bonds. The markouts said they were right about the direction and wrong about the ratio: the equity fell more than the bonds, as the capital-structure algebra predicts when the debt is money-good. The hand history goes in the file. *(The trade is illustrative.)*

- **Private credit is public credit with the price removed.** Same borrowers, same sponsors, two pricing regimes. The difference is measurement, not credit.
- **A mark is a moving average of the truth.** Reported volatility is deflated by $\sqrt{\sum_k\theta_k^2}$, contemporaneous beta by $\theta_0$, and the Sharpe ratio is inflated by $1/\sqrt{\sum_k\theta_k^2}$. NAV momentum is a property of the valuation calendar.
- **Sum the lags.** The Dimson aggregated beta recovers the true beta, and the lagged coefficients forecast the next mark from public data you already have.
- **Unsmooth gently.** Inverting a kernel with $\theta=0.7$ amplifies measurement noise more than sixteen times. Pool across co-holders and report intervals.
- **One discount point is half an asset point.** $m=\big((1-\phi)-P/\text{NAV}\big)/(1+\ell)$: at 1.1x leverage, a 20% equity discount says the loans are worth about 90, not 80.
- **The non-accrual pair hides a mark.** $\hat R^{\text{mark}}_{\text{NA}}=(w^{FV}/w^{C})(FV/C)$; a rising cost-minus-fair-value gap with a falling headline rate is the hole getting deeper.
- **A 5% cap rations a run; it does not stop one.** Requesting dominates once $m>0$ is believed, the transfer is $p\cdot m$ per quarter, and the request percentage is the best public belief series in the asset class.
- **Trade the wrappers.** BDC equity, BDC bonds, ETFs with firm bids, CDX Financials, the loans semi-liquid funds sell and the supply private takeouts create. IDO or it didn't happen.

### The Spec You Hand the Robot

**Vague version.** "ROBO, minimize the mark gap." ROBO writes to the valuation committee recommending that all loans be marked to the listed BDC's implied price, which minimizes the gap to zero and the manager's fee base by 10%. It did exactly what was asked.

**Precise version: the Mark-Gap Monitor.**

- **Inputs.** `bdc_quarterly`, `soi`, `redemptions` and `public_index` with the §17.2 schemas; quarterly frequency; decimals, not percent strings; net (not gross) debt to NAV; NAV vintage stored alongside each restatement.
- **Step 1, kernel.** For each cluster of co-holding vehicles, fit $\hat\theta$ by pooled Dimson regression with $K\le3$, requiring $10(K+1)$ observations; bootstrap quarters in blocks of four; refuse a point estimate if the 90% interval for $\theta_0$ is wider than 0.4.
- **Step 2, pending mark.** $\Pi_{i,t}=\hat\beta_i\sum_{j=0}^{K-1}\bar\Theta_{j+1}F_{t-j}$ using the vehicle's sector-matched public index.
- **Step 3, implied markdown.** $m_{i,t}=\max\big(0,((1-\phi_i)-P/\text{NAV})/(1+\ell_i)\big)$ on buyback-adjusted forward NAV; NaN for non-traded vehicles, never 1.0.
- **Step 4, gap and features.** $G_{i,t}=m_{i,t}-\max(0,-\Pi_{i,t})$; regress cross-sectionally on software share, bad-PIK share, stale-mark share, cross-holder dispersion, non-accrual gap $g_t$, borrower count and the sibling redemption request percentage; output the residual.
- **Step 5, runway.** For every semi-liquid vehicle, $\mathcal{T}$ with repayments taken from the §17.4 hazard model under the current regime; flag $\mathcal{T}<5$ quarters.
- **Outputs.** One row per (`bdc_id`, `qdate`): $\hat\theta$ with interval, $\Pi$, $m$, $G$, residual signal, $\mathcal{T}$ and every flag that fired. Units in column names.
- **Tests.** All five blocks' sanity checks in this chapter, plus a restatement test (a restated NAV must not change any earlier row's signal) and a non-traded test (no P/NAV, no $m$, no signal, but a runway).

### Exercises

1. **The year-long lag.** A manager's marks recognize a true return evenly over four quarters, $\theta_k=1/4$ for $k=0,\dots,3$. Show that the reported Sharpe ratio is twice the true one and that $\rho^o_1=3/4$. ROBO reports the vehicle's annualized volatility as 2.1%. What is the true figure, and what correlation with the loan index should you expect contemporaneously and after summing three lags?
2. **Marking the discount.** A listed BDC trades at 0.62 of NAV with net leverage 1.25x and an estimated fee drag of 4%. Compute $m$. Then argue, without computing, whether the true markdown is higher or lower once you admit that the BDC's unsecured notes are not money-good, and say which chapter's model you would use to find out.
3. **The bad bucket.** A BDC reports non-accruals of 3.1% at cost and 1.0% at fair value, with portfolio fair value at 97% of cost. What is the implied carrying value of its non-accrual loans? Compare it with the roughly 50-cent restructuring recoveries Octus reported in April 2026, and state which number you would put in a Chapter 14 recovery model, and why neither is a recovery.
4. **Kaz's fix.** Kaz proposes eliminating redemption queues by raising the cap to 100%. With requests at 40% of shares and a true markdown of 8%, compute the stayers' true value per share under a 5% cap and under Kaz's 100% cap. Then explain why the 100% cap does not end the game but changes it into a classic bank run, and what Diamond and Dybvig would have told him.
5. **Takeout season.** Using block 3, find the regime value $\zeta$ at which expected private-to-syndicated supply halves relative to $\zeta=0$. Then show that the naive supply estimate overstates the competing-risks one by more in the tight regime, and explain why that matters for a CLO-demand forecast.
6. **The thirteen-week model, reborn.** Take any perpetual BDC's latest 10-Q and fill in Theo's runway: cash, undrawn lines (net of any borrowing-base exclusion for PIK or non-accrual loans), the syndicated sleeve, unfunded commitments, debt maturities and trailing repayments. How many quarters of 5% redemptions can it fund? Now cut repayments by half, as in the 2022–2024 tight regime, and recompute. Write down what the credit agreement says about the borrowing base before you trust either number.

# Part V: Market Microstructure, Portfolio Trading, ETFs & Loans

*Chapters 18–22*

Equities are a supermarket. Every item has a price tag, there is one checkout, and the queue is visible to everyone. Corporate credit is a bazaar. There are no price tags; every price is a negotiation; the merchant studies your face while you study the rug; and if you ask three stalls for a quote on the same rug, all three now know something about you. Electronification is the slow installation of barcode scanners, one stall at a time. The ETF is a supermarket built next to the bazaar that sells sealed boxes of bazaar goods at a posted price, and the people who open the boxes for a living are called authorized participants. The loan market is the stall at the back where you agree a price today and the rug arrives in three weeks, maybe.

Ines runs this part of the book, because it is a poker room with worse lighting. "In the bazaar the merchant reads your face," she says. "On the RFQ, the merchant reads your hand history. Be the merchant."

**Chapter 18, OTC Credit Microstructure & the Market Maker's Equations,** is the core derivation of the book's market-making half. It walks through Harris's taxonomy of traders, the Roll, Glosten–Milgrom, and Kyle models of the spread, and then the Avellaneda–Stoikov and Guéant–Lehalle–Fernandez-Tapia machinery in full (the HJB equation, the exponential-utility ansatz, the reservation price $r^{\text{res}}$, the optimal spread) before adapting it to the thing credit actually is: RFQs rather than limit order books, win probabilities that depend on the distance to a composite price, inventory that cannot be unwound at will, and a jump-to-default term that adds $q\lambda J$ to the reservation price. It decodes TRACE, measures RFQ hit rates, and treats BWIC leakage as the information problem it is.

**Chapter 19, Portfolio Trading & Basket Pricing Engines,** prices a 150-line portfolio trade in ninety seconds: the sum of fair values, less liquidation costs, less a risk charge on the residual covariance over the unwind horizon, which requires a covariance matrix for bonds that have not traded this month, a factor model and shrinkage to make it invertible, an eviction rule for the lines you refuse, a stress model for liquidity that becomes correlated exactly when you need it not to, and a healthy fear of the mystery box, the basket assembled by someone who knows which lines are the problem.

**Chapter 20, Credit ETF Creation/Redemption Arbitrage (HYG, JNK, LQD, BKLN),** explains how the sealed boxes get made and unmade: authorized participants, custom baskets, bid-side NAV, the arbitrage bands set by creation and redemption costs, ETF price as the market's real-time estimate when the bonds themselves are not trading, and March 2020, when the boxes traded at discounts that looked like a malfunction and were in fact the only honest price on the screen.

**Chapter 21, Leveraged Loans, CLOs & Loan-Market Microstructure (TREND),** is the back stall: settlement that takes weeks, CLO constraints (CCC buckets, overcollateralization and interest-coverage tests) that turn vehicles into forced sellers on a schedule, repricing waves, the halting arrival of loan e-trading, and the loan and CLO ETFs that now sit on top of a market never designed for daily liquidity.

**Chapter 22, Market-Structure Regulation & the Forces Reshaping Liquidity (TREND),** takes each rule that changed the plumbing (TRACE reporting-time changes, T+1 settlement, the Treasury clearing mandate, Basel III endgame and dealer capital, CDS reporting and clearing) and works through what it did to the economics of a desk.

The trend that defines this part is that the basket became the unit of liquidity. Single bonds still trade one at a time, by negotiation, but an increasing share of risk moves in portfolios and ETF creation units, priced by engines in seconds, and the data exhaust from those trades is the raw material for everything in Part III. Mags, asked about this, says that back in her day you could get a two-way market on a single bond by calling someone who owed you a favor, and that it was worse, and that she misses it.

# Chapter 18: OTC Credit Microstructure & the Market Maker's Equations

*11:52 a.m.* The RFQ arrived the way bad news always arrives on a credit desk: politely, in a grey box, with a countdown timer. *Client sells \$8mm Halvorsen Packaging 7.25% Senior Secured Notes due 2029 (a fictional issuer; B2/B), disclosed, five dealers in competition, three minutes to respond.* The composite said 91.25.

Kaz's auto-quoter had already filled in a bid of 90.875. "Avellaneda–Stoikov," Kaz said, with the calm of someone whose model has never been subpoenaed. "We're long three million already. Twenty-day realized vol, half-spread from the fitted win curve, rounded to the nearest eighth, because this market is a medieval guild."

Theo had the indenture open on his second monitor, because he always had a credit document open on his second monitor. "Their lender call is at noon," he said. "And the indenture lets them buy back notes below par through open market purchases, with no cap. If they announce a discounted repurchase at noon, today's sellers are the people who were told first."

"Is an open market purchase like open outcry?" Kaz asked. "Do they have to shout?"

"They have to pay less than you," Theo said.

"So the seller may know something," said Ines, without looking up. "What's the pot, what are the odds, and who at this table knows more than you?"

"The client," Theo said. "Maybe four of the five dealers. Definitely not the auto-quoter."

From across the row, Mags did not look up either. "Back in my day we'd just not pick up the phone."

Ines dragged the bid to 90.25 and sent it. It did not trade; someone covered at 90.50. Twenty minutes later the bond was 86 bid, and the chat windows filled with the noise a market makes when it finds out who the patsy was. On \$8mm, the winner had just bought a \$360,000 lesson *(illustrative)*.

Kaz stared at the screen. "The model was right about the inventory."

"The model was right about the part you asked it about," Ines said. "A quote is four things glued together. You priced one."

That is the question this chapter answers: *what is the right bid, and how much of it is fear, how much greed, how much suspicion, and how much the price of being asked again tomorrow?*

By the end of this chapter you will be able to: map Harris's trader taxonomy onto the credit ecosystem and say who is a forced seller to whom; estimate an effective spread from TRACE prints with Roll's trick, and know when the estimator is lying; derive Kyle's $\lambda$ and estimate it from markouts; derive the Avellaneda–Stoikov (AS) quotes from the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) equation without skipping steps; solve the Guéant–Lehalle–Fernandez-Tapia (GLFT) inventory-bounded problem as a linear ODE system; extend both to jump-to-default; fit an RFQ win curve and price a hit-ratio target; decode a TRACE file into features; and model a BWIC as a first-price auction with a leaky list. You will also be able to hand all of it to ROBO in a spec that leaves it nothing to guess.

## 18.1 Harris's Zoo, Relabeled for Credit

A restructuring banker learns to ask *who holds the paper and what are they forced to do*. A market maker asks the same question, but at the speed of a timer and about everyone at once. Larry Harris's *Trading and Exchanges* (2003), the standard practitioner text on market microstructure, sorts traders by *why* they trade. **Utilitarian traders** trade for some reason other than profiting from the trade itself: hedging, investing cash, meeting a redemption, or obeying a regulator. **Profit-motivated traders** trade because they think the price is wrong or about to move. These include the *informed*, who know something about value; *order anticipators*, who know something about other people's orders; and *bluffers*, who want you to believe they know something. Between them stand the **dealers**, who sell immediacy, and the **arbitrageurs**, who sell convergence. Harris adds four dimensions of liquidity: **immediacy** (how fast you can trade), **width** (the cost of a round trip), **depth** (how much size you can do at that cost), and **resiliency** (how fast the price recovers after you trade).

Relabeled for the credit ecosystem of Chapter 1, the zoo looks like this.

| Harris type | Credit population (2026) | What they want | What they cost the dealer |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Utilitarian, uninformed | Insurers selling fallen angels for capital reasons; index funds at month-end; CLOs curing CCC buckets; LDI-linked holders meeting margin calls | Immediacy at a fair price, predictably timed | Little in expectation. This is the dealer's bread. |
| Utilitarian, arbitrage | ETF authorized participants (Chapter 20); portfolio-trade desks (Chapter 19); CDS–bond basis traders | Convergence of a basket to its NAV | Basket risk and the mystery-box problem, but rarely issuer-level information |
| Profit-motivated, mostly uninformed about issuers | Systematic factor pods trading momentum, value, and carry baskets (Chapters 9–11) | Factor exposure | Factor beta, which the dealer can hedge. IDO or it didn't happen: their markouts are mostly not toxic once you strip the factor. |
| Profit-motivated, informed | Distressed and crossover funds; LMT participants; anyone who has actually read the indenture | To trade before the information is in the price | The residual markout, which is the whole adverse-selection problem |
| Order anticipators | Anyone who has seen a BWIC list, a leaked run, or a large RFQ shopped to too many dealers (§18.9) | To trade ahead of known flow | Pre-auction drift, paid by the seller |
| Dealers | Bank dealers; non-bank liquidity providers, about 10% of credit market-making revenue in 2024 *(approx.; industry dossier)* | Spread, and future flow | Competition. Non-banks bring a different $\gamma$ and a different $k$ (§18.4). |

Harris's four liquidity dimensions turn into the four things an RFQ engine must estimate before it answers anything. Immediacy is the *win probability* within the timer. Width is the *reservation spread* plus the markup. Depth is how the reservation price changes with *block size*, not just with one more lot. Resiliency is the *impact decay* after a print, which is the spring Paleologo describes for equities (Paleologo p.152–153). In bonds the spring is the dealer's own inventory, and it relaxes only when the dealer finds the other side. The rest of the chapter derives a model for each.

> **Desk Myth vs. Desk Reality.** *Myth:* "The bid–ask spread is the dealer's profit." *Reality:* The quoted spread is four charges, and only one of them is profit. **Fear** is the inventory risk premium, $\gamma\sigma^2(T-t)$ in §18.4. **Greed** is the markup a dealer with some pricing power can charge, $\tfrac{2}{\gamma}\ln(1+\gamma/k)$. **Suspicion** is the expected adverse markout, $2\pi\sigma_V$ in Glosten–Milgrom (§18.3). **Franchise** is a *negative* charge: the subsidy a dealer pays to keep winning enough RFQs to stay on the client's list (§18.7). Realized profit is the spread minus the markout. On a toxic RFQ it is negative, which is why "the dealer made the spread" is something only people who have never been a dealer say.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Man_Quantitative_Credit_Alpha_Early_Mover_2022 p.19:* "the bond market is structured around a Request for Quotation (RFQ) process that has hardly changed for decades. Corporate bond bid/ask prices are indicated by dealer runs that are not firm and actionable"
>
> **Annotation.** Our analysis: the Man authors are right about the *protocol* and, by 2026, wrong about the *responder*. The disclosed RFQ is still a sealed-bid auction among a handful of dealers. What changed between 2022 and 2026 is who answers it. Trumid reported 88% of eligible RFQ line items executed with no human touch in September 2025, and Tradeweb says AiEX now handles a large and rising share of its institutional trades (sources in Trend Watch, §18.7). The runs are still "not firm and actionable", which is why §18.2 has to recover spreads from prints rather than quotes. The same page also complains about "if filled" trades. That complaint is the reason the modern engine treats fill probability as a modeled variable rather than as noise: in §18.7 the win curve $P(x)$ is a first-class input to the quote, not an afterthought in the backtest.

## 18.2 Roll's Trick: Seeing the Spread When No One Will Show You One

Equities show you a spread. Credit shows you a *print*, fifteen minutes late, with the size capped and the side sometimes ambiguous, and asks you to infer the spread from it, like a sommelier asked to name the vintage from the cork. Roll (1984), "A Simple Implicit Measure of the Effective Bid-Ask Spread in an Efficient Market" (*Journal of Finance* 39(4)), found that the spread leaves a fingerprint in the *autocovariance* of price changes. A trade at the bid tends to be followed by a trade at the ask, so prices bounce, and the bounce is negatively autocorrelated.

### 18.2.1 Derivation

Let $m_t$ be the efficient mid, a random walk $m_t = m_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$ with $\varepsilon_t$ i.i.d., mean zero, variance $\sigma_\varepsilon^2$. Let $I_t \in \{-1,+1\}$ indicate whether print $t$ was a customer sell (at the bid) or a customer buy (at the ask). Let $c = S/2$ be the effective half-spread in price points. The print is

$$
p_t = m_t + c\,I_t .
$$

Then $\Delta p_t = \varepsilon_t + c\,(I_t - I_{t-1})$. Assume first, as Roll did, that $I_t$ is i.i.d. with $\mathbb{P}(I_t = 1) = \tfrac12$, independent of $\varepsilon$. Then $\text{Var}(I_t) = 1$ and all cross-covariances vanish, so

$$
\text{Cov}(\Delta p_t, \Delta p_{t+1}) = c^2\,\text{Cov}(I_t - I_{t-1},\, I_{t+1} - I_t) = -c^2\,\text{Var}(I_t) = -\frac{S^2}{4}.
$$

Solving for the spread gives Roll's estimator:

$$
\widehat{S}^{\text{Roll}} = 2\sqrt{-\widehat{\text{Cov}}(\Delta p_t, \Delta p_{t+1})}.
$$

Bao, Pan & Wang (2011), "The Illiquidity of Corporate Bonds" (*Journal of Finance* 66(3)), use the same covariance directly as an illiquidity measure, $\gamma^{\text{BPW}} = -\text{Cov}(\Delta p_t,\Delta p_{t+1})$ computed on TRACE prices. They find bond illiquidity far larger than quoted spreads suggest, and priced in the cross-section. (Their $\gamma$ is not our risk aversion $\gamma$, hence the superscript.)

Now break the assumption the way credit breaks it. Large customer orders are *split*: a \$25mm sell goes out as five \$5mm RFQs over an afternoon. Model the trade signs as a symmetric two-state Markov chain with lag-one autocorrelation $\rho \in [0,1)$, so that $\text{Cov}(I_t, I_{t+j}) = \rho^{|j|}$. Expanding term by term,

$$
\text{Cov}(I_t - I_{t-1},\, I_{t+1} - I_t) = \rho - 1 - \rho^2 + \rho = -(1-\rho)^2,
$$

so $\text{Cov}(\Delta p_t,\Delta p_{t+1}) = -c^2(1-\rho)^2$ and

$$
\widehat{S}^{\text{Roll}} \;\to\; S\,(1-\rho).
$$

Order splitting makes Roll *underestimate* the spread by the factor $(1-\rho)$. Add informed flow that moves the mid in the direction of the trade over several prints, so that the $\varepsilon_t$ are positively autocorrelated, and the covariance can turn positive. The square root then has no real solution. That is not a numerical accident. It is the estimator telling you that the bounce has been overwhelmed by momentum, which is information in its own right (§18.3). Dynkin's team makes the same point from the other side when it uses return autocorrelation as an illiquidity proxy: investors split trades, which produces positive autocorrelation, and stale prices do the same (Dynkin p.771).

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Ben_Dor_Quantitative_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.120:* "for most bonds the time between a broker-dealer buy and sell transaction for a given CUSIP can be very long, so it is difficult to calculate an accurate bid-ask spread using TRACE."
>
> **Annotation.** Our analysis: this is the practical objection to Roll in credit, and it bites harder than it looks. Roll's algebra assumes the mid barely moves between consecutive prints, so that $\sigma_\varepsilon^2$ is small next to $c^2$. When a dealer's round trip spans three days, the mid diffuses between prints and the bounce is buried. The covariance estimate is unbiased in theory and useless in practice, because its standard error scales with $\text{Var}(\Delta p)$, which is now dominated by $\sigma_\varepsilon^2$. Ben Dor's team responded by building Liquidity Cost Scores from trader *indications* rather than prints. The 2026 desk has a third option the 2010 authors lacked: dense electronic RFQ logs, its own and the platforms', where both sides of the market are observed within seconds. Use Roll on TRACE as a cross-check and a stress indicator, not as your spread.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Dynkin_Systematic_Investing_in_Credit p.702:* LCS "measures the cost of an immediate round-trip transaction of a typical institutional size and is expressed as a percentage of a bond price"
>
> **Annotation.** Our analysis: notice the three qualifiers, *immediate*, *round-trip*, and *typical institutional size*. Roll measures none of them exactly: it measures the average bounce across whatever sizes printed, with no immediacy constraint. For spread-quoted bonds, LCS is the bid–offer spread times spread duration. Ben Dor p.123 then multiplies the indications of non-benchmark bonds by an adjustment factor between 1.50 and 1.83, which is the industry admitting in writing that dealer indications are tighter than dealer markets. The modern desk uses LCS-type composites as the prior and its own RFQ fills as the likelihood.

> **Trend Watch: the great spread compression, and its stress reversals (2004–2026).** *What changed:* TRACE dissemination was phased in from 2002 to 2005. Edwards, Harris & Piwowar (2007, *Journal of Finance* 62(3)) and Goldstein, Hotchkiss & Sirri (2007, *Review of Financial Studies* 20(2)) find that transparency helped liquidity, though not uniformly: the first reports lower trading costs once TRACE disseminates prices, and the second a neutral-to-positive effect, with spreads narrowing except for very large trades and very infrequently traded bonds (magnitudes vary by sample and bond type; see the papers). *How big, then:* Chen, Lesmond & Wei (2007) estimate bid–ask spreads of about 25 bp for AAA bonds and 180 bp for CCC; Man's 2022 authors note that spreads are "markedly tighter in the current market" (Man_Quantitative_Credit_Alpha_Early_Mover_2022 p.20). *The stress reversal:* the same Man page charts a 20-day average HY bid–ask (Bloomberg data, 1 July 2017 to 2 February 2021) that gaps out in February–March 2020 and then normalizes. Kargar et al. (2021, *Review of Financial Studies*) estimate that at the March 2020 peak, customers' willingness to pay for immediacy rose by roughly 200 bp per dollar traded, and flow shifted from risky-principal to slower agency trades. *2026:* MarketAxess data reported by The DESK (2026-10-01) show the median EUR IG bid–ask down from 0.0879 to 0.0673 price % of par (−23.5%), comparing the 34 weeks to 2026-08-23 with the same weeks of 2025. In the March 2026 stress, however, EUR IG bid–ask hit 64% above its January average, and recovery took 4 weeks (EUR IG), 6 (US HY), 8 (US IG), 13 (EUR HY), and 14 (EM, which then widened again and has been above its January level in 21 of the 22 weeks since the peak). *What it means for the desk:* the median spread is a fair-weather number. A cost model calibrated on a calm window, by Roll or anything else, underprices exactly the trades you most need to price. Make the spread estimator regime-conditional, and carry the stress multiplier as a parameter.

> **Ways This Blows Up.** (1) *Taking the absolute value.* When the sample covariance is positive, someone always writes `2*sqrt(abs(cov))`. That reports a spread when the data are reporting momentum. Return NaN and log the sign. (2) *Mixing sizes.* Odd lots pay more than blocks (Edwards, Harris & Piwowar 2007), and "5MM+" capped prints are a different market from \$50k retail prints. Estimate by size bucket. (3) *Interdealer double counting.* Both dealers report an interdealer trade. Leave both legs in and you manufacture a bounce of exactly zero width between two identical prices, which biases the covariance toward zero (§18.8). (4) *Stale prints.* Prints days apart measure diffusion, not bounce. Cap the gap between consecutive prints or weight by it.

### Specification for AI Implementation (Roll estimator)

**The Spec You Hand the Robot.** *What ROBO built from the vague version ("estimate the bid–ask spread from TRACE"):* it averaged (ask print − bid print) over all prints on the same day, on a bond that traded twice a week, and reported a spread of zero for every day with one print. The precise spec: input a time-ordered vector of cleaned prices (points per 100 par) for one bond and one size bucket. Output `(spread, autocov)` in points. Require at least `min_obs` price changes. Return `NaN` when the autocovariance is non-negative, and never take an absolute value. Sanity checks: recover a known spread on simulated Roll data, recover $S(1-\rho)$ under order splitting, and return `NaN` under momentum.

The third check is worth working by hand. With $S = 0.10$ and $\rho = 0.6$, the bounce contributes $-c^2(1-\rho)^2 = -0.0025 \times 0.16 = -0.0004$ to the autocovariance. The mid increments have stationary variance $0.01/(1-0.16) \approx 0.0119$ and lag-one autocovariance $0.4 \times 0.0119 \approx 0.0048$. Momentum wins by a factor of twelve, and a well-behaved estimator says so by refusing to answer.

## 18.3 Who Knows More Than You: Glosten–Milgrom Recalled, Kyle Derived

Roll measured the spread and assumed nobody knew anything. The next two models put knowledge back in. Glosten–Milgrom asks *whether* the person on the other side knows more than you. Kyle asks *how much* their size tells you. In an RFQ market you get to see both the side and the size before you quote, which is a gift Kyle's market maker never received, and also a trap, because the client knows you are looking.

### 18.3.1 Glosten–Milgrom in one line

Chapter 3 derived the RFQ version. Let the bond's value be $V = m \pm \sigma_V$ with equal probability, and let a fraction $\pi$ of RFQs come from clients who know which. A zero-profit dealer sets each quote to the conditional expectation of value given the side of the trade:

$$
p^{b} = \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[V \mid \text{client sells}] = m - \pi\sigma_V, \qquad p^{a} = m + \pi\sigma_V .
$$

The suspicion spread is $2\pi\sigma_V$. It is the price of not knowing which hand you are facing, and it exists even for a dealer with zero inventory and zero risk aversion. Remember that fact for §18.5, where dealer inventory goes to zero and the spread does not.

### 18.3.2 Kyle (1985), derived

Kyle's market maker does not see individual orders. It sees only the total order flow. One informed trader knows the liquidation value $v \sim \mathcal{N}(p_0, \Sigma_0)$, with $\sigma_v = \sqrt{\Sigma_0}$. Noise traders submit $u \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_u^2)$, independent of $v$. The insider submits $x$, the market maker sees $y = x + u$ and sets a price $p$ equal to $\mathbb{E}[v \mid y]$, and the insider maximizes expected profit $\mathbb{E}[(v - p)\,x \mid v]$.

*Notation.* The book reserves $\lambda$ for default intensity. Kyle's price-impact slope is therefore $\lambda^{K}$.

Guess linear strategies: $x = \beta(v - p_0)$ and $p = p_0 + \lambda^{K} y$.

*Insider's problem.* Given $v$, the insider chooses $x$ to maximize $\mathbb{E}[x(v - p_0 - \lambda^{K}(x + u))] = x(v - p_0) - \lambda^{K}x^2$. The first-order condition gives

$$
x = \frac{v - p_0}{2\lambda^{K}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \beta = \frac{1}{2\lambda^{K}} .
$$

*Market maker's problem.* Projection of $v$ on $y$ gives

$$
\lambda^{K} = \frac{\text{Cov}(v, y)}{\text{Var}(y)} = \frac{\beta\Sigma_0}{\beta^2\Sigma_0 + \sigma_u^2}.
$$

*Fixed point.* Substitute $\beta = 1/(2\lambda^{K})$:

$$
\lambda^{K}\left(\frac{\Sigma_0}{4(\lambda^{K})^2} + \sigma_u^2\right) = \frac{\Sigma_0}{2\lambda^{K}}
\;\Longrightarrow\; \lambda^{K}\sigma_u^2 = \frac{\Sigma_0}{4\lambda^{K}}
\;\Longrightarrow\; \lambda^{K} = \frac{\sigma_v}{2\sigma_u}, \qquad \beta = \frac{\sigma_u}{\sigma_v}.
$$

Market depth is $1/\lambda^{K}$: the flow needed to move the price one point. The posterior variance is $\text{Var}(v \mid y) = \Sigma_0/2$, so the trade reveals exactly half of the insider's information. The insider earns $\mathbb{E}[x(v-p)] = \tfrac12\sigma_v\sigma_u$, which the noise traders pay, while the market maker breaks even. The insider scales trading to the amount of camouflage: double the noise and the insider trades twice as much, at the same impact per unit of private information. That is why informed credit flow loves month-end and index rebalance days.

### 18.3.3 Translating Kyle to the RFQ

Three changes turn Kyle into a desk tool.

1. **Flow is observed per client, not in aggregate.** On a disclosed RFQ the dealer sees the client's name, side, and size. The noise-versus-informed split that Kyle hides in $u$ is now a *classification problem by client tier*. Glosten–Milgrom's $\pi$ becomes $\pi_c$, estimated from that client's hand history.
2. **The value $v$ is a future IDO-adjusted mid.** Define the $h$-day markout of trade $i$ as the change in the bond's mid from the trade time to $h$ days later, after stripping the rates move and the bond's factor-model prediction (Chapter 9). A markout that is factor beta is not information about the issuer. IDO or it didn't happen.
3. **Estimate $\lambda^{K}$ by regression.** Regress markouts on signed size normalized by average daily volume:

$$
\text{MO}_{i,h} = a_h + \lambda^{K}_{h}\,\frac{y_i}{\text{ADV}_i} + \mathbf{b}_h^{\top}\mathbf{z}_i + e_{i,h},
$$

where $y_i > 0$ is a customer buy and $\mathbf{z}_i$ holds controls (rating, age, ETF flow, time of day). Use $h \in \{1, 5, 20\}$ days. The regression on the move from the *pre-trade* mid recovers the information content $\lambda^{K}$. Run the same regression on the move from the *trade price* and an efficient dealer should see a slope of zero. A positive post-trade slope means the street under-reacted to the flow, and the bond *drifts* after informed trades. A negative slope means the street over-reacted, or charged for inventory, and the price *bounces back*.

This is momentum and reversal at the microstructure scale, and it is the same fork Chapter 10 meets at monthly horizons. Post-RFQ drift is momentum conditional on informed flow. Roll's bounce is reversal conditional on uninformed flow. The desk's job is to tell them apart in three seconds.

Guo, Lehalle & Xu (2021), *Transaction Cost Analytics for Corporate Bonds* (arXiv 1903.09140), estimate exactly this kind of curve on Enhanced TRACE. The transient impact jumps at the trade and then decays toward a permanent level. In the language of this chapter, the jump is the dealer's suspicion and inventory charge, the decay is Harris's resiliency, and the permanent level is Kyle's information. Their headline finding is an *asymmetry* between customer-buy and customer-sell impact, which a symmetric $\lambda^{K}$ cannot capture. Estimate $\lambda^{K}_{\text{buy}}$ and $\lambda^{K}_{\text{sell}}$ separately.

> **Poker Table.** Ines draws it on a napkin. "The number of dealers in comp is the number of players. The size is the bet. The client's name is the tell. And the cover, the second-best price you only learn after you lose, is the hand you didn't get to see." Winning an RFQ against four other dealers means you were the most optimistic of five people looking at the same cards. "If you win every hand at a five-handed table," she says, "you aren't good. You are the one paying for everyone's information." Hendershott & Madhavan (2015, *Journal of Finance* 70(1)) find that electronic auctions are used mainly for smaller, more liquid, less information-sensitive trades, while larger tickets go to voice, where fewer players see the cards. Fermanian, Guéant & Pu (2017, arXiv 1511.07773) model one European dealer's multi-dealer-to-client RFQ data and find that dealers quote more conservatively as the number of requested dealers rises. That is the winner's curse, priced in at the table (§18.9 does the arithmetic).

### Specification for AI Implementation (Kyle estimator)

Input: arrays of markouts (points, IDO-adjusted, horizon $h$ stated in the column name) and signed flow (customer buy positive; USD mm or ADV-normalized; state which). Output: slope and $t$-statistic. In production, use heteroskedasticity-robust errors clustered by issuer and day. The simulation below checks the closed form, the absence of post-trade drift under efficient pricing, and the insider's profit $\tfrac12\sigma_v\sigma_u$.

## 18.4 Avellaneda–Stoikov, Derived Without Skipping Steps

Kaz's auto-quoter was an Avellaneda–Stoikov engine. Avellaneda & Stoikov (2008), "High-frequency trading in a limit order book" (*Quantitative Finance* 8(3): 217–224), built on the dealer-inventory model of Ho & Stoll (1981). It is the most-cited model on the desk and the least-read. We read it now, one step at a time.

### 18.4.1 Setup

Work under $\mathbb{P}$, with time in years.

- **Mid.** $dS_t = \sigma\,dW_t$, arithmetic Brownian motion in price points. Here $\sigma$ is in points per $\sqrt{\text{yr}}$. (Jumps are added in §18.6.)
- **Quotes.** The dealer posts a bid $p^b_t = S_t - \delta^b_t$ and an ask $p^a_t = S_t + \delta^a_t$, with $\delta^b,\delta^a$ in points.
- **Fills.** Counting processes $N^b_t$ and $N^a_t$ jump by one lot when the bid or ask is hit, with intensities $\Lambda(\delta^b_t)$ and $\Lambda(\delta^a_t)$, where $\Lambda(\delta) = A e^{-k\delta}$. $A$ is the arrival rate at zero distance (RFQs per year per side), and $k$ (per point) is how fast business decays as you quote away.
- **Inventory and cash.** $q_t = N^b_t - N^a_t$ in lots, and $dX_t = p^a_t\,dN^a_t - p^b_t\,dN^b_t$.
- **Objective.** Exponential utility of terminal wealth, with risk aversion $\gamma$ per point-lot:

$$
u(t,x,s,q) = \sup_{\delta^b,\delta^a}\; \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}_t\!\left[-\exp\!\big(-\gamma(X_T + q_T S_T)\big)\right].
$$

### 18.4.2 The HJB equation

Dynamic programming gives the diffusion term from $S$ and one jump term per counting process. When the bid is hit, cash falls by $s - \delta^b$ and inventory rises by one; when the ask is lifted, cash rises by $s + \delta^a$ and inventory falls by one:

$$
\partial_t u + \tfrac12\sigma^2\partial_{ss}u
+ \sup_{\delta^b}\Lambda(\delta^b)\big[u(t,x - s + \delta^b, s, q+1) - u\big]
+ \sup_{\delta^a}\Lambda(\delta^a)\big[u(t,x + s + \delta^a, s, q-1) - u\big] = 0,
$$

with terminal condition $u(T,x,s,q) = -\exp(-\gamma(x + qs))$.

### 18.4.3 Step 1: the frozen-inventory value and the reservation prices

Suppose first that the dealer cannot trade. Using $\mathbb{E}[e^{aZ}] = e^{a^2/2}$ for standard normal $Z$, with $\tau = T - t$,

$$
v(t,x,s,q) = \mathbb{E}\big[-e^{-\gamma(x + qS_T)}\big] = -\exp\!\Big(-\gamma x - \gamma q s + \tfrac12\gamma^2 q^2\sigma^2\tau\Big).
$$

The **reservation bid** $r^b$ is the price at which the dealer is indifferent to buying one more lot: $v(t, x - r^b, s, q+1) = v(t,x,s,q)$. Equating exponents,

$$
\gamma r^b - \gamma s + \tfrac12\gamma^2\sigma^2\tau\big[(q+1)^2 - q^2\big] = 0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
r^b = s - (1+2q)\,\frac{\gamma\sigma^2\tau}{2}.
$$

The same argument for selling one lot gives $r^a = s + (1-2q)\,\gamma\sigma^2\tau/2$. Their average is the famous **reservation price**:

$$
r^{\text{res}} = s - q\,\gamma\sigma^2\tau. \tag{18.1}
$$

A long dealer ($q>0$) values the bond below the mid, and by an amount proportional to inventory, risk aversion, variance, and time left. This is the skew.

### 18.4.4 Step 2: the exponential ansatz

Try $u = -\exp(-\gamma(x + \theta(t,s,q)))$ with $\theta(T,s,q) = qs$. Then $\partial_t u = -\gamma u\,\theta_t$ and $\partial_{ss}u = u(\gamma^2\theta_s^2 - \gamma\theta_{ss})$. The jump terms factor as

$$
u(t, x - s + \delta^b, s, q+1) - u = u\left[e^{-\gamma(\delta^b - s + r^b)} - 1\right], \qquad r^b \equiv \theta(t,s,q+1) - \theta(t,s,q),
$$

and similarly on the ask, with $r^a \equiv \theta(t,s,q) - \theta(t,s,q-1)$. These $r^b, r^a$ are the indifference prices of the *true* value function, not of the frozen one. Because $u<0$, dividing the HJB by $-\gamma u > 0$ preserves the supremum and gives

$$
\theta_t + \tfrac12\sigma^2\theta_{ss} - \tfrac12\gamma\sigma^2\theta_s^2
+ \sup_{\delta^b}\frac{\Lambda(\delta^b)}{\gamma}\Big[1 - e^{-\gamma(\delta^b - (s - r^b))}\Big]
+ \sup_{\delta^a}\frac{\Lambda(\delta^a)}{\gamma}\Big[1 - e^{-\gamma(\delta^a - (r^a - s))}\Big] = 0 .
$$

Read the bracket on the bid: $\delta^b - (s - r^b) = r^b - p^b$ is the profit from buying at $p^b$, measured at the dealer's own reservation value, passed through the utility.

### 18.4.5 Step 3: the first-order condition

Write $y = \delta - \Delta$, with $\Delta = s - r^b$ on the bid. Maximize $f(\delta) = \Lambda(\delta)(1 - e^{-\gamma y})$. Setting $f'(\delta) = 0$:

$$
\Lambda'(\delta)\big(1 - e^{-\gamma y}\big) + \gamma\Lambda(\delta)e^{-\gamma y} = 0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
y^{*} = \frac{1}{\gamma}\ln\!\left(1 - \gamma\,\frac{\Lambda(\delta^*)}{\Lambda'(\delta^*)}\right). \tag{18.2}
$$

Equation (18.2) holds for *any* decreasing intensity, and §18.7 uses it with a logistic win curve. Since $f = 0$ at $y = 0$, $f \to 0$ as $\delta \to \infty$, and $f > 0$ in between, the unique critical point is a maximum. For the exponential intensity, $\Lambda'/\Lambda = -k$, so

$$
p^{b} = r^{b} - \frac{1}{\gamma}\ln\!\Big(1 + \frac{\gamma}{k}\Big), \qquad
p^{a} = r^{a} + \frac{1}{\gamma}\ln\!\Big(1 + \frac{\gamma}{k}\Big). \tag{18.3}
$$

The parameter $A$ has cancelled: how *often* you are asked does not enter the markup. Hold that thought.

### 18.4.6 Step 4: the AS approximation, and the two halves of the spread

The exact $r^b, r^a$ require solving for $\theta$ (GLFT do this in §18.5). Avellaneda and Stoikov approximate them by the frozen-inventory values of Step 1, which is accurate when $\gamma$ or the fill intensity is small. Substituting:

$$
p^{b} = s - \big(q + \tfrac12\big)\gamma\sigma^2\tau - \frac{1}{\gamma}\ln\!\Big(1+\frac{\gamma}{k}\Big),
\qquad
p^{a} = s - \big(q - \tfrac12\big)\gamma\sigma^2\tau + \frac{1}{\gamma}\ln\!\Big(1+\frac{\gamma}{k}\Big),
$$

$$
p^{a} - p^{b} = \underbrace{\gamma\sigma^2\tau}_{\text{fear}} + \underbrace{\frac{2}{\gamma}\ln\!\Big(1+\frac{\gamma}{k}\Big)}_{\text{greed}}. \tag{18.4}
$$

*Limit 1: $\gamma \to 0$.* A Taylor expansion gives $\tfrac{1}{\gamma}\ln(1+\gamma/k) = \tfrac1k - \tfrac{\gamma}{2k^2} + O(\gamma^2) \to \tfrac1k$. A risk-neutral dealer facing demand $Ae^{-k\delta}$ maximizes $\delta A e^{-k\delta}$, whose maximizer is $\delta^{*} = 1/k$. So the second half of the spread is the monopoly markup. It is pure market power, and $k$ is the price elasticity of your RFQ wins. A more competitive market (larger $k$) means a smaller markup, and a dealer with no risk aversion still charges it.

*Limit 2: $t \to T$.* The fear term and the skew both vanish. The AS dealer becomes fearless at the bell.

**Worked example (the cold open).** Take $\sigma = 8$ points$/\sqrt{\text{yr}}$, which is roughly what a B2 bond with spread duration near 4 and spread volatility near 200 bp a year implies *(illustrative)*. Take $\tau = 5/252$ years, a one-week expected holding period rather than the time to the close. Take $\gamma = 0.005$ per point-lot, with a lot of \$1mm, so the dealer's risk tolerance $1/\gamma$ is 200 point-lots, or \$2mm. Take $k = 3$ per point and $q = +3$. Then $\sigma^2\tau = 1.270$ point$^2$, so the fear per lot is $\gamma\sigma^2\tau = 0.0063$ points and the inventory part of the bid distance is $(q+\tfrac12)\gamma\sigma^2\tau = 0.022$ points. The greed per side is $200\ln(1.001667) = 0.333$ points. The bid is $91.25 - 0.022 - 0.333 = 90.895$, which rounds to 90.875 on the eighths grid. That is Kaz's quote.

Notice the proportions: Kaz's quote was 94% greed and 6% fear. In a bond, the diffusive inventory term is usually pennies. The AS dealer is a monopolist with a nervous tic. The real fear lives in jumps (§18.6) and in the client (§18.7), neither of which the formula was given.

> **Units box: what ROBO did with the volatility.** $\sigma$ is the price volatility of the mid in **points per $\sqrt{\text{yr}}$**; $\tau$ is in **years**; $\gamma$ is per **point × lot**; $k$ is per **point**; $q$ is in **lots** (state the lot size); $A$ is in **RFQs per year per side**. Convert spread volatility to price volatility with $\sigma_P \approx D^{\text{spr}}\,P\,\sigma_s$, where $\sigma_s$ is the decimal spread volatility; for $D^{\text{spr}} = 4$, $P = 91.25$ and $\sigma_s = 0.02$, that gives $\sigma_P \approx 7.3$ points. ROBO was told "use the bond's volatility" and fed 200, the spread vol in bp. The fear term rose by a factor of 625, and the bid came out at 77.03 on a bond at 91.25. ROBO was, technically, being prudent.

> **Ways This Blows Up.** (1) *Terminal time is a calendar artifact.* With $T$ set to 4 p.m., the skew collapses into the close, so the dealer gets brave at 3:55 p.m., the least liquid minutes of the HY day. Set $\tau$ to the expected holding period or use the stationary GLFT quotes (§18.5). (2) *The skew can cross the market.* The spread in (18.4) is positive, but the center $r^{\text{res}}$ moves by $q\gamma\sigma^2\tau$. A desk short 50 lots can produce a bid above the composite offer. Clip quotes to a band around the composite and route breaches to a human. (3) *$A$ does not enter.* AS quotes the same in a bond asked about once a month as in one asked about a hundred times a day. For illiquid bonds this is plainly wrong, and §18.5 fixes it. (4) *$\sigma$ must be a $\mathbb{P}$ forecast of mid price volatility* over the holding period, not CDS implied vol and not spread vol in bp. (5) *The exponential intensity is local.* A real RFQ win curve saturates at one when you bid through the composite. Use (18.2) with the fitted curve (§18.7). (6) *One lot is not a block.* AS prices the marginal lot. The client is selling eight (§18.7).

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Ben_Dor_Quantitative_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.120:* "If a trader were temporarily long inventory of a particular bond, then the trader might quote the bond with a tighter spread (i.e., a higher offered spread) to entice a bid, and vice versa."
>
> **Annotation.** Our analysis: this is the AS skew observed in the wild, written down by people who wanted to remove it. A long trader moves the offer toward the bid to attract buyers, which in spread terms means raising the offered spread. That is (18.1) acting on one side of the market. To Ben Dor's team the skew is contamination in a liquidity measure, and they average a month of indications to wash it out. To a market maker it is the optimal policy, and it carries information: a dealer whose runs skew persistently toward selling a bond is telling you its inventory. The 2026 desk can turn the observation around and estimate street inventory from the skew of composite contributors, then use it as a feature (§18.8). One caveat about the quotation's world: these were indications, not firm quotes. A dealer can skew a run for free; a firm streaming quote has to pay for the skew when it is hit.

### Specification for AI Implementation (AS quoting core)

**The Spec You Hand the Robot.** *Vague version:* "quote bonds using Avellaneda–Stoikov." *What ROBO built:* $T$ = 4 p.m. New York, so its quotes widened at 9:30 a.m. and tightened all afternoon, and its σ came from the CDS ladder. *Precise version:* inputs are the composite mid $s$ (points), inventory $q$ (lots of \$1mm), price volatility $\sigma$ (points/$\sqrt{\text{yr}}$, 20-day $\mathbb{P}$ forecast), $\gamma$ (per point-lot), $k$ (per point, from the fitted win curve), and holding-period horizon $\tau$ (years, never the time to the close). Outputs are bid, ask, $r^{\text{res}}$, and the fear and greed split, all in points, plus prices rounded to the instrument's tick. Guards: reject negative inputs; use the $1/k$ limit when $\gamma < 10^{-12}$; never let unit conversion happen inside the function.
