# Appendix B: The Data & API Atlas

It is 11:40 p.m. Theo Marsh has fourteen browser tabs open and a spreadsheet called `data_sources_FINAL_v3.xlsx`.

"TRACE has every corporate bond trade," he says. "EDGAR has every credit agreement. FRED has the high-yield spread back to the nineties. So I can rebuild the credit market from public data and go home."

Ines Okafor doesn't look up. "Which of those rows did you check this week? A trade over \$5 million shows up on the tape as `5MM+`. The credit agreement is filed with its schedules left out and the pricing grid redacted. And since April, the FRED series you love keeps only three years of history. Every dataset is a hand history with some cards face down. Your job is to know which ones."

Mags Dunleavy, coat on: "Back in my day the data source was a guy named Lenny. Lenny had survivorship bias too. He only remembered the trades that worked."

ROBO, asked to "get all the bond data," has queued 4.1 million requests to `data.sec.gov` with no User-Agent header. It is about to find out what a 403 is.

Keep this appendix open next to every other chapter. By the end you will be able to name each source's access, cost, and signal-carrying fields; list how each one lies (staleness, survivorship, look-ahead, caps, licensing); quantify and undo stale-price bias; and give ROBO a testable bond-panel schema. Every URL was checked on 2026-10-17. Sources we could not check have no link.

## B.0 How to Read an Atlas Entry (and Four Ways Data Lies)

Each entry gives **what it is**, **access & cost**, **key fields**, **gotchas**, and **used in**. Four failure modes come up in almost every entry, so we state them formally once. ROBO cannot enforce a vibe.

**Sin 1: Stale prices.** Let $r_t$ be the true log return, i.i.d. with variance $\sigma^2$. Suppose the observed price only partially adjusts each day: $p^{o}_t = (1-\theta)\,p_t + \theta\,p^{o}_{t-1}$, where $\theta\in[0,1)$ measures staleness. Then

$$r^{o}_t = (1-\theta)\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \theta^{k} r_{t-k}, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(r^{o}_t) = (1-\theta)^2 \sigma^2 \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\theta^{2k} = \frac{1-\theta}{1+\theta}\,\sigma^2 .$$

The lag-$h$ autocovariance is $\gamma_h = \theta^{h}\operatorname{Var}(r^o_t)$, so $\rho_1=\theta$. The long-run variance is untouched:

$$\sum_{h=-\infty}^{\infty}\gamma_h = \frac{1-\theta}{1+\theta}\sigma^2\Big(1 + \tfrac{2\theta}{1-\theta}\Big) = \sigma^2 .$$

Staleness does not remove risk. It spreads today's risk over the following days. With $\theta=0.6$, a bond shows 25% of its true daily variance (half the volatility) and 60% first-order autocorrelation. Betas take the same hit. If $r_t=\beta f_t+\epsilon_t$ and the factor is observed fresh, then $\operatorname{Cov}(r^o_t,f_{t-k})=(1-\theta)\theta^k\beta\sigma_f^2$. A contemporaneous regression recovers only $(1-\theta)\beta$. The Dimson (1979) sum of lagged betas recovers $\beta$, because $\sum_k(1-\theta)\theta^k=1$. This is part of why high-yield bonds look rate-insensitive in daily data (Chapter 8). A stale price is a calm price, and calm is the most expensive thing to be wrong about.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Ben_Dor_Quantitative_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.208:* "we attempt to directly identify and exclude observations that possibly reflect stale prices. Specifically, all bonds comprising the Corporate and High Yield indexes with a sequence of five or more unchanged quotes in any month are excluded from the eligible population of bonds for that month."
>
> **Annotation.** The Barclays team used two fixes. Sampling biweekly instead of daily lowers the effective $\theta$, and a run-length filter removes bonds whose quotes don't move. The run-length rule still screens *evaluated* prices well, but a TRACE price carried forward is one old trade copied onto later rows, so our schema carries an explicit `days_stale` counter (§B.16). The derivation shows what the filter buys you: dropping the bonds with high $\theta$ pushes measured variance and beta back toward the truth. The price is a tilt toward liquid names, which is a factor exposure of its own (Chapter 9).

**Sin 2: Look-ahead.** A feature $X_{i,t}$ is admissible only if $X_{i,t}\in\mathcal{F}_t$. In code, that means you join on `knowledge_ts` (when you could have known it), never `effective_ts` (the date the value refers to). Some examples. A TRACE print executed at 4:58 p.m. and reported at 5:12 p.m. is known at 5:12. A downgrade effective Tuesday and published Thursday is known Thursday. An XBRL fact is known when the filing is accepted.

**Sin 3: Survivorship.** The universe at date $t$ is every bond that existed and was eligible at $t$, including bonds that later defaulted, were called, tendered, or matured. Today's index constituents, today's ETF holdings, and any "active securities" table are survivor-biased. In credit, the bonds that drop out are the defaulted ones, and they *are* the left tail.

**Sin 4: Licensing.** Ratings, CUSIPs, index levels, and composites come with contracts that limit storage, redistribution, and derived products. If you can't legally keep the data behind a backtest, you can't audit the backtest. That is a model risk.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Man_Quantitative_Credit_Alpha_Early_Mover_2022 p.20:* "It is necessary to combine information from a number of different data sources in order to build up a picture of the price landscape in the credit markets. These include data from market runs, electronic platforms, TRACE data and dealer information."
>
> **Annotation.** No single source gives you the price. This appendix sorts the sources into three kinds: *public and lagged* (TRACE), *proprietary and fresh* (platform RFQs, dealer runs), and *model outputs* (composites, evaluated prices). If a model treats all three as interchangeable "prices," the noise in one leaks into labels built from another.

## B.1 FINRA TRACE: The Tape

**What it is.** FINRA's reporting and dissemination system for OTC fixed-income trades. It launched July 1, 2002, with a 75-minute deadline that fell to 15 minutes by July 1, 2005. All public corporate trades have been disseminated on receipt since January 9, 2006. Agency and primary-market trades were added in 2010, ABS/MBS in 2011, 144A dissemination in 2014, and Treasury reporting in 2017. *(Source: FINRA, TRACE Fact Book 2025, <https://www.finra.org/sites/default/files/2026-02/TRACE_FactBook_2025.pdf>.)*

**Access & cost.** TRACE comes in four layers, from freshest to most complete:

1. **Real-time feeds.** The Bond Trade Dissemination Service (BTDS) is the real-time corporate feed. Agency, securitized-product, and 144A trades have their own feeds. You license it from FINRA or, more often, through a market-data vendor, and it is priced like professional market data. We could not retrieve the current BTDS spec or fee schedule this session, so check both before you build a feed handler.
2. **Free views.** FINRA's site shows disseminated trades for individual bonds. The API Developer Center (<https://developer.finra.org/>) has a Query API and a dataset catalog. This is the public tape: sizes are capped and dealers are not identified.
3. **Enhanced Historical Data (EHD).** EHD includes "information previously not disseminated to the public, such as buy/sell indicators and counterparty (dealer or customer) information," and quantity "as reported and not subject to dissemination caps." FINRA "makes historical data available 6 months (18 months for Securitized Products) after the transaction date and publishes the information quarterly" (FINRA EHD product sheet, <https://www.finra.org/sites/default/files/TRACE_Enhanced_Historical_Data.pdf>). Coverage: corporate and 144A from July 1, 2002, agency from April 2010, structured products from May 2011. You need a Historical Data Agreement and pay fees. CUSIP and non-CUSIP versions are offered, the latter "for customers without a CUSIP license" (<https://www.finra.org/filing-reporting/trace/historic-academic-data>). Materials from 2016–2017 quote an 18-month corporate lag. The current page says 6.
4. **Academic Corporate Bond TRACE Data.** Available only to higher-education institutions, "on a 36-month delayed basis," with "masked identifying information regarding the dealer reporting each transaction." It includes 144A and non-disseminated trades. At launch the fee was \$500 per year plus a \$500 one-time set-up fee (FINRA Regulatory Notice 16-43, <https://www.finra.org/sites/default/files/notice_doc_file_ref/Regulatory-Notice-16-43.pdf>). Masked dealer IDs make dealer-network and inventory research possible, but nothing like them exists in production. Keep it on the research side of the wall.

Most researchers get TRACE Standard, Enhanced, and 144A tables through **WRDS**.

**Key fields.** CUSIP and FINRA symbol; execution date and time; *report* date and time; price; yield; quantity (capped publicly, true in EHD); buy/sell side; reporting- and contra-party type (dealer or customer); principal or agency capacity; commission flag; trade status and message sequence numbers; as-of and special-condition flags; ATS identifier; and the portfolio-trade modifier (from May 15, 2023).

**Dissemination caps.** On the public tape, investment-grade and unrated trades above \$5 million print as `5MM+`, and high-yield trades above \$1 million print as `1MM+`. True sizes appear only in historical products.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Ben_Dor_Quantitative_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.162:* "TRACE ... disseminates trade-by-trade corporate bond execution information within 15 minutes to all market participants. At this time, TRACE data are censored at \$5 million for investment grade and \$1 million for high-yield securities."
>
> **Annotation.** "Censored" is the statistically correct word. A capped print is right-censored, so volume sums and VWAPs built from the public tape are skewed toward small trades, and small trades tend to print on the wrong side of the spread. A 2026 desk does three things about it. It flags every capped print. It imputes true size from a tail fitted to EHD, for example a Pareto tail conditional on exceeding the cap. And it never trains on public-tape volumes while scoring on EHD volumes. One more trap: the cap depends on the rating *at trade time*. A fallen angel's cap drops from \$5mm to \$1mm on the day the downgrade becomes known, and §B.16 tests for exactly this.

**Reporting timing: the one-minute saga.** The 15-minute outer limit has applied to corporates since 2005. On September 20, 2024, the SEC approved SR-FINRA-2024-004, which cut the limit to one minute for fully electronic trades. Manual trades got a phase-in (15 minutes, then 10, then 5), and firms with fewer than 4,000 reported trades a year were exempt. "FINRA has not implemented the changes approved in File No. SR-FINRA-2024-004." On September 16, 2025, the SEC approved SR-FINRA-2025-008, which *keeps* the 15-minute limit. The same filing lets dual broker-dealer/investment-adviser firms report the allocations of an aggregate order as a single report that includes the number of accounts (Release No. 34-103986, <https://public-inspection.federalregister.gov/2025-18147.pdf>). The record shows 82.9% of eligible trades executed between 8:00 a.m. and 6:15 p.m. were already reported within one minute in 2022. The rule targeted the slow 17%: blocks and voice trades, where the information is. Rule 6730 also sets 60 minutes for Treasuries, post-issuance CMOs, and specified pools; same day for CDOs and CMBS executed by 5:00 p.m.; and T+1 for List/Fixed Offering Price and Takedown trades (<https://www.finra.org/rules-guidance/rulebooks/finra-rules/6730>).

**What is *not* disseminated.** Under Rule 6750 (<https://www.finra.org/rules-guidance/rulebooks/finra-rules/6750>): affiliate trades; certain M&A transfers; List/Fixed Offering Price and Takedown trades; CMBS, CDOs, and CMOs that don't qualify for periodic dissemination; foreign sovereigns; and Treasuries other than on-the-run nominal coupons. Those on-the-run coupons have been disseminated end-of-day since March 25, 2024, with size caps, no participant IDs, and free next-day access for non-professional use (Regulatory Notice 24-06). CLO tranches fall under the CDO exclusion. They are *reported* to TRACE but not disseminated by transaction, so no public CLO tape exists.

**Gotchas.**
- *The tape is messages, not trades.* Cancellations, corrections, and reversals must be matched to the original by message sequence number. The rules differ before and after FINRA's February 2012 re-platform (Dick-Nielsen 2009, 2014).
- *Double counting.* An inter-dealer trade is reported by both sides, and agency trades can print twice.
- *Fat fingers.* Decimal shifts (1012.5 for 101.25) and one-print spikes that bounce back need explicit screens.
- *Two clocks.* Execution time and report time differ. A late report on a block is information in itself.
- *Settlement.* US corporates settle T+1 since May 28, 2024. Accrue interest to settlement date.

**Used in.** Chapters 2, 3, 7, 8, 9, 18, 19, 20, 22.

> **Trend Watch. The tape that almost got faster (2018–2026).** FINRA added transparency at the edges. Covered depository institutions began reporting Treasury, agency, and MBS trades on September 1, 2022. The portfolio-trade modifier and 60-minute Treasury reporting arrived May 15, 2023, and USD foreign sovereigns became reportable on November 6, 2023 (TRACE Fact Book 2025). End-of-day transaction data for on-the-run Treasuries began March 25, 2024. The historical corporate lag shrank from 18 months to 6. The core corporate tape, though, went in a circle. One-minute reporting was approved September 20, 2024, never implemented, and replaced on September 16, 2025, by a 15-minute limit plus aggregate allocation reporting. The MSRB rolled back the same day (SR-MSRB-2025-01). The 2018 SEC advisory-committee proposal to raise caps (up to \$10mm IG) has not changed the public tape. **Desk implication:** the 15-minute window and the caps are the information asymmetry your market-making model prices (Chapter 18). Treat both as fixed until a rule changes them. Keep the PT flag as a feature, because PT prints are priced as part of a basket, not bond by bond (Chapter 19).

## B.2 SEC EDGAR: The Legal Prose Warehouse

**What it is.** The SEC's filing system, holding 10-K and 10-Q financials (with XBRL), 8-K event disclosures, and the debt contracts filed as exhibits.

**Access & cost.** Free. The `data.sec.gov` APIs "do not require any authentication or API keys to access" (<https://www.sec.gov/edgar/sec-api-documentation>). `CIK##########` below is the zero-padded 10-digit CIK.
- Submissions: `https://data.sec.gov/submissions/CIK##########.json` ("typical processing delay of less than a second").
- Company facts: `https://data.sec.gov/api/xbrl/companyfacts/CIK##########.json`. Company concept: `.../api/xbrl/companyconcept/CIK##########/us-gaap/<Tag>.json`.
- Frames: `https://data.sec.gov/api/xbrl/frames/us-gaap/AccountsPayableCurrent/USD/CY2019Q1I.json`. Periods are written `CY2019` (annual), `CY2019Q1` (quarterly), and `CY2019Q1I` (instantaneous).
- Bulk files `companyfacts.zip` and `submissions.zip` are rebuilt nightly (around 3:00 a.m. ET). Use them for any large pull.

XBRL endpoints usually lag under a minute. There is no CORS support, so run your code server-side. Fair-access rules (<https://www.sec.gov/os/accessing-edgar-data>): "Current max request rate: 10 requests/second," and every request must carry a declared User-Agent of the form `Sample Company Name AdminContact@<sample company domain>.com`.

**Full-text search** (<https://www.sec.gov/edgar/search/efts-faq.html>) covers all electronic filings "since 2001," including "all attachments (such as exhibits)." It supports exact phrases, `OR`, `NOT`, `NEAR(n)` (default 10 words), and trailing wildcards. Its backing JSON endpoint (`efts.sec.gov`) is undocumented. Use it for J.Crew-blocker screens, e.g., *unrestricted subsidiary* NEAR(5) *intellectual property* (Chapter 13).

**Credit-document exhibits** (Regulation S-K Item 601, <https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/17/229.601>): **EX-4** (indentures, supplemental indentures); **EX-10** ("every contract not made in the ordinary course of business that is material," which includes credit agreements, amendments, intercreditors, and joinders, usually attached to an 8-K under Item 1.01 or 2.03, or to a 10-Q); **EX-21** (subsidiaries, your starting point for the restricted/unrestricted map).

**Gotchas.**
- *The 10% hole.* Long-term debt that "does not exceed 10 percent of the total assets of the registrant and its subsidiaries on a consolidated basis" need not be filed (Item 601(b)(4)(iii)(A)).
- *Redactions.* Schedules may be omitted if they are listed (Item 601(a)(5)). Terms that are "both not material and is the type that the registrant treats as private or confidential" may be redacted (Item 601(b)(10)(iv)). Pricing grids often show up as `[***]`, so give your parser a redaction token.
- *Private issuers.* Issuers whose debt is 144A-for-life file nothing. Their documents sit in lender data rooms, on the private side.
- *XBRL look-ahead.* Frames returns, for each entity, the fact "that is last filed," so restatements overwrite originals. Rebuild point-in-time values from `companyfacts` using each fact's accession number and `filed` date, or better, the acceptance timestamp from submissions. Debt details often sit in custom extension tags that frames won't return.

**Used in.** Chapters 11, 13, 15, 25, 26.

## B.3 CourtListener, RECAP, PACER, and the Claims Agents

**What it is.** PACER is the judiciary's pay-per-page docket system. Free Law Project's CourtListener hosts the **RECAP Archive**, which mirrors PACER documents that users of the RECAP browser extension have already paid for. Claims agents run free case websites with dockets and claims registers.

**Access & cost.**
- **PACER** (<https://pacer.uscourts.gov/pacer-pricing-how-fees-work>): \$0.10 per page, capped at \$3 per document. The cap does not cover search results or reports that aren't case-specific. Audio is \$2.40 a file and opinions are free. Fees are waived in any quarter where you spend \$30 or less. Every docket refresh is billed again, so pull mega-case dockets incrementally with date filters.
- **CourtListener REST API v4** (docs now on the Free Law Project wiki, <https://wiki.free.law/c/courtlistener/help/api/rest/v4/overview>). Base URL `https://www.courtlistener.com/api/rest/v4/`. Authenticate with the header `Authorization: Token <token>`; the docs warn that "a common mistake is to forget the word 'Token'." Current defaults: "authenticated users may make up to 5 requests per minute, 50 requests per hour, and 125 requests per day," on a rolling window, with higher limits available through membership or commercial agreements. Use webhooks for docket alerts rather than polling.
- **RECAP Fetch** (<https://wiki.free.law/c/courtlistener/help/api/rest/v4/recap>): `POST /api/rest/v4/recap-fetch/` with `request_type` 1 (docket), 2 (PDF), or 3 (attachment page). It "uses your PACER credentials to purchase and download PACER content," runs asynchronously, and allows 30 requests a minute. The upload endpoint is "not available to the public."
- **Python.** `juriscraper` (<https://github.com/freelawproject/juriscraper>, BSD-2, Python 3.11+) parses court sites and "a variety of pages and reports within the PACER system."
- **Claims agents.** Stretto (<https://cases.stretto.com/>), Epiq (<https://dm.epiq11.com/>), and Verita Global (<https://www.veritaglobal.com/>), whose CaseView links point to the legacy KCC domain. Kroll Restructuring Administration (formerly Prime Clerk) and Omni Agent Solutions are the other majors; we could not open their sites this session. Agent sites are free, usually update faster than RECAP, and post claims registers in structured form.

**Key fields.** Dockets: court, case number, `pacer_case_id`, filing date, judge, parties, attorneys. Entries: number, date, description, and documents with `pacer_doc_id`. Claims: claim number, creditor, debtor entity, amount, priority (secured, 503(b)(9), priority, GUC), date filed. Rule 2019 statements become a time series of who is in the ad hoc group (Chapter 25).

> **Docket Diary.** A document is in RECAP only if someone with the extension bought it, so coverage favors mega-cases and misses the small-cap Chapter 11 your model needs. *The Ad Hoc Group, represented by counsel, notes that its Rule 2019 statement was amended four times and RECAP holds two of the versions.*

**Gotchas.** Docket text is free-form, so the same motion can carry a dozen different descriptions. Claim amounts are as *asserted*, not as allowed, and duplicate claims filed against several debtor entities inflate the totals. For look-ahead purposes, the right timestamp is when the entry appeared on the docket, not the date printed inside the PDF.

**Used in.** Chapters 13, 14, 16, 25.

## B.4 MSRB EMMA

**What it is.** EMMA (<https://emma.msrb.org/>) is the MSRB's free site for municipal trade data, official statements, continuing disclosures, statistics, and yield curves. Real-time and historical feeds are sold as MSRB subscriptions. Rule G-14 requires reporting to RTRS "as soon as practicable but no later than 15 minutes after the Time of Trade" (<https://www.msrb.org/Rules-and-Interpretations/MSRB-Rules/General/Rule-G-14>). One-minute amendments were approved September 20, 2024, and rescinded September 16, 2025.

**Gotchas.** Munis mask large trade sizes under their own conventions, so check RTRS dissemination rules before reusing TRACE cleaning code. Most issues almost never trade, which makes staleness worse than in HY corporates. A late continuing-disclosure filing is itself a credit signal.

**Used in.** Chapters 12, 22.

## B.5 CME Treasury Futures, MDP 3.0, and BrokerTec

**What it is.** CME lists the Treasury futures used for rate hedging (2-, 5-, and 10-year, Ultra 10-year, Bond, and Ultra Bond). It also owns **BrokerTec**, the inter-dealer central limit order book for cash Treasuries and repo, acquired with NEX Group in 2018. The real-time protocol is **MDP 3.0**: UDP multicast, Simple Binary Encoding (SBE), incremental and snapshot-recovery channels, and market-by-price and market-by-order books. History is sold through CME DataMine. CME's site blocked automated checks this session, so no deep links.

**Access & cost.** Exchange licensing is per device or per enterprise, and an algorithm consuming the feed triggers non-display fees. DataMine is priced per dataset.

**Key fields.** Contract and expiry, book levels and sizes, trades with the aggressor side, sequence numbers, exchange timestamps, settlement prices, and open interest. Add the deliverable basket and conversion factors, which you need for cheapest-to-deliver (CTD) and futures DV01 (Chapters 8, 24).

**Gotchas.** When you see a sequence gap, recover from the snapshot channel; never interpolate across it. Futures DV01 jumps when the CTD changes. Rolls move liquidity between contracts, and back-adjusted series give correct returns but wrong levels. BrokerTec shows only the inter-dealer market. Client flow, which is where the information is, trades on dealer-to-client RFQ platforms.

**Used in.** Chapters 8, 22, 24, 27.

## B.6 OPRA, Cboe, and Options Data

**What it is.** **OPRA** (<https://www.opraplan.com/>) is the securities information processor for US listed options. It disseminates consolidated "last sale and quotation information," volume, open interest, and end-of-day summaries from BOX, Cboe, MEMX, MIAX, Nasdaq, and NYSE options venues. Its 2026 notices add IEX Options and MX2 Options, extend trading hours effective September 21, 2026, and upgrade hardware. **Cboe DataShop** (<https://datashop.cboe.com/>) sells Option EOD Summary (with a 3:45 p.m. ET snapshot), interval Option Quotes, and Option Trades, with optional implied volatility and Greeks and an academic discount. OptionMetrics IvyDB, usually through WRDS, is the academic standard for volatility surfaces.

**Access & cost.** OPRA charges vendor and subscriber fees under its fee schedule. For credit work, a daily or 3:45 p.m. surface snapshot per issuer is enough for Merton/CreditGrades inputs, put-vs-CDS comparisons, and skew-implied jump-to-default (Chapter 23).

**Gotchas.** The options "close" is a quote snapshot, and it isn't synchronized with the equity close, which produces false put-call parity violations. Early exercise and dividends bias naive Black–Scholes implied vols in the deep out-of-the-money puts that carry the default signal.

**Used in.** Chapters 8, 23, 27.

## B.7 Index Data: ICE BofA, Bloomberg, iBoxx/CDX/iTraxx, and FRED

**What it is.**
- **ICE BofA** (<https://www.ice.com/fixed-income-data-services/index-solutions>): "over 6,000" fixed-income indices, including US High Yield (H0A0) and US Corporate (C0A0). ICE says its index history on Snowflake Marketplace spans "50 years."
- **Bloomberg** (the former Lehman/Barclays family): Aggregate, Corporate, High Yield, and the Very Liquid versions. JNK tracks the Bloomberg High Yield Very Liquid Index.
- **iBoxx, CDX, iTraxx** belong to S&P Global since its 2022 merger with IHS Markit. HYG tracks the iBoxx USD Liquid High Yield Index. CDX and iTraxx roll to a new series every six months.
- **FRED** republishes ICE BofA OAS: **BAMLH0A0HYM2** (HY, <https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/BAMLH0A0HYM2>) and **BAMLC0A0CM** (IG, <https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/BAMLC0A0CM>). On 2026-10-15 they were 3.23% and 0.84%, i.e., 323 bp and 84 bp (FRED, accessed 2026-10-17). The FRED API (<https://fred.stlouisfed.org/docs/api/fred/>) includes `fred/series/vintagedates` for real-time vintages.

**Access & cost.** Constituent-level data is licensed and expensive; index-level series are cheaper.

**Gotchas.**
- *Month-end rebalancing.* A bond downgraded mid-month stays in the IG index until the month-end rebalance, and fallen-angel selling clusters on those dates (Chapter 9).
- *Index prices are evaluated, bid-side prices* (§B.8). Index OAS is smoothed, so §B.0 applies.
- *Excess-return definitions differ.* Some families use duration-matched Treasuries, others swaps. Don't mix them in one regression.
- *CDX rolls.* An on-the-run series jumps in level on the roll date, so splice explicitly.
- *FRED is shrinking.* The series notes now say "Starting in April 2026, this series will only include 3 years of observations. For more data, go to the source." ICE's notes add that the data is "provided for your internal use only."

**Used in.** Chapters 2, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 20.

> **Trend Watch. Free data giveth, and free data taketh away (2018–2026).** In 2018 one line of `pandas-datareader` pulled decades of daily HY OAS from FRED. Since April 2026, FRED keeps three years and sends you "to the source," while ICE sells 50 years of history on Snowflake. CourtListener's default authenticated allowance is now 125 requests a day. Academic open data went the other way. The Open Source Bond Asset Pricing project released TRACE-based panels and factor libraries, with its Stage 1 daily panel in public beta on 2025-12-11, and FINRA's EHD corporate lag fell to 6 months. **Desk implication:** cache everything free in a versioned, point-in-time local store, because free data disappears. License what production depends on. Reconcile the open panels against vendor data so you notice when either one drifts.

## B.8 Composite and Evaluated Pricing: Model Outputs Dressed as Prices

**What it is.**
- **MarketAxess CP+** (<https://www.marketaxess.com/price/cp-plus>) covers IG, HY, EM, loans, munis, sovereigns, and rates. It is built from "proprietary MarketAxess trading activity, TRACE, TraX, and other market signals," including inquiries that never traded. MarketAxess says it prices "80% more bonds than public sources alone," and delivers via FIX API, OMS feeds, and an Excel add-in.
- **Tradeweb Ai-Price** is a machine-learning price for bonds that haven't traded recently, with confidence measures. **Bloomberg BVAL** is an evaluated price with a BVAL Score that grades how much market evidence supports it. **ICE evaluated pricing**, including continuous evaluated pricing, is the incumbent for fund NAVs. Others include S&P Global and LSEG evaluated pricing and BondCliQ quotes. We could not open the Tradeweb, Bloomberg, or ICE pricing pages this session, so read their methodology documents before you depend on them.

**Access & cost.** Enterprise licenses, with limits on redistribution and on how long you may store the data.

**Key fields.** Bid, mid, and ask; timestamp; confidence or score; methodology tier (based on trades vs. based on comparable bonds).

**Gotchas.**
- *Circularity.* Composites are built partly from TRACE. If you train on composite labels with TRACE features, part of what you predict is your own input. Validate on *subsequent* trades (markouts).
- *Staleness.* A bond with no new information follows its comparables, so its $\theta$ sits well above zero. Use the score field to set observation weights.
- *Bid-side NAVs.* Credit ETF NAVs are struck from bid-side evaluated prices. In March 2020, part of the "discount" of HYG and LQD to NAV was the NAV being stale (Chapter 20).

**Used in.** Chapters 7, 18, 19, 20.

> **Trend Watch. Pricing became a product (2018–2026).** Venues turned order-flow data into pricing products (CP+, Ai-Price). Portfolio trades, flagged in TRACE since May 15, 2023, are priced and marked up against composite mids (Chapter 19). **Desk implication:** your engine competes with the composites. Log both on every RFQ and prove your edge in markouts.

## B.9 Ratings-Agency Default Studies

**What it is.** S&P Global Ratings publishes an annual global corporate default and rating-transition study. Moody's publishes an annual study of corporate default and recovery rates since 1920. Fitch publishes default studies and loan and HY default indices. SEC Rule 17g-7(b) requires rating agencies to publish their rating-action histories in XBRL, with a lag, which gives you free (if awkward) point-in-time ratings.

**Access & cost.** Summaries are often free after registration. Full data and production rating feeds are licensed. The trace-data-pipeline public download leaves out some columns "because agency ratings are licensed."

**Gotchas.** Results depend on how a study handles withdrawn ratings. Distressed exchanges count as defaults (S&P "SD"; Moody's distressed exchanges). In the LMT era that changes the recovery distribution and leads to re-defaults (Chapter 14). Default rates are physical-measure, through-the-cycle numbers. Using them as $\mathbb{Q}$ hazards without a risk premium understates spreads, which is the credit spread puzzle (Chapter 6). Join ratings on publication time, not effective date.

**Used in.** Chapters 5, 6, 11, 14.

## B.10 Academic Bond Panels: OBAP, WRDS Bond Returns, Mergent FISD

**Open Source Bond Asset Pricing** (<https://openbondassetpricing.com/>), run by Alexander Dickerson and coauthors, publishes "108 Bond Factors," 341 factors from *Factor Investing with Delays*, a bond-level ML panel with 341 predictors (2002-07 to 2022-12), duration-matched Treasury returns, and replication packages. Its **trace-data-pipeline** (<https://github.com/Alexander-M-Dickerson/trace-data-pipeline>, MIT license) works in stages. Stage 0 turns Enhanced, Standard, and 144A TRACE into daily panels using Dick-Nielsen (2009, 2014) and van Binsbergen–Nozawa–Schwert (2025) filters, a decimal-shift corrector (10×, 0.1×, 100×, 0.01×), a bounce-back filter, agency de-duplication, and an ultra-distressed flag. Stage 1 adds QuantLib analytics, ratings, and FISD terms. Stage 2 builds 108 monthly signals. Stages 0–1 need WRDS. §B.16 is a teaching-scale version of Stages 0–1.

**WRDS Bond Returns** (<https://wrds-www.wharton.upenn.edu/pages/grid-items/wrds-bond-returns/>) is a monthly panel of prices, returns, coupons, and yields built from TRACE Standard and Enhanced, starting July 2002, with a bond-to-equity link table built through CRSP. Its month-end price rule, meaning which late-month trade counts as the month-end price, moves measured reversal and factor premia. That sensitivity is the subject of Dickerson et al., *The Corporate Bond Factor Replication Crisis*.

**Mergent FISD** (via WRDS) is the academic security master. It holds offering terms, coupon type, maturity, seniority, 144A and convertible flags, call, put, and sink schedules, covenant indicators, and histories of amount outstanding and ratings. **Gotchas:** coverage of small and private issues is patchy. Amount-outstanding updates lag tenders and exchanges, and in an LMT the change in amount outstanding *is* the event. CUSIPs are licensed.

**Used in.** Chapters 7, 9, 10, 11.

## B.11 Leveraged Loans and CLOs

**What it is.** There is no public loan tape. In *Kirschner v. JPMorgan Chase* (2d Cir. 2023), the court held that the syndicated term-loan notes at issue were not securities. The sources you have: the **LSTA** (<https://www.lsta.org/>), which publishes market analysis such as its *BSL Market Monthly* (built on the Morningstar LSTA Leveraged Loan Index), settlement standards, and documentation; PitchBook LCD for new issues and defaults; and dealer-quote mark services such as LSEG's. CLO data comes from Intex (waterfalls), monthly trustee reports (collateral, OC/IC tests, CCC buckets), rating-agency surveillance, and Creditflux's CLO-i. TRACE collects CLO tranche trades but does not disseminate them (§B.1).

**Gotchas.** Loan "prices" are averages of dealer quotes, not trades. Repricings and amend-and-extends change a loan's terms without changing its identifier. Trustee reports arrive monthly and late, so the forced-seller signal from a CCC bucket (Chapter 21) is about a month stale.

**Used in.** Chapters 12, 16, 17, 21.

## B.12 ETF Holdings Files

**What it is.** Under SEC Rule 6c-11 (2019), most US ETFs post full holdings every day. iShares pages include "Download latest fund holdings CSV data." HYG (<https://www.ishares.com/us/products/239565/ishares-iboxx-high-yield-corporate-bond-etf>) launched April 4, 2007. SPDR pages offer a daily `.xlsx`. JNK (<https://www.ssga.com/us/en/intermediary/etfs/spdr-bloomberg-high-yield-bond-etf-jnk>) launched November 28, 2007. The files are free to download, and each sponsor's terms govern redistribution.

**Key fields.** As-of date, name, identifiers (ISIN, sometimes CUSIP), par, market value, weight, price, and sector, plus coupon, maturity, duration, and yield for bond funds. Layouts differ, so write and test one parser per sponsor.

**Gotchas.** The holdings file is not the creation basket, because custom baskets are allowed (Chapter 20). Each file overwrites the last one. If you don't archive daily, you have no history and every backtest is survivor-biased. Cash, futures, and CDS overlays need special handling.

**Used in.** Chapters 2, 19, 20.

## B.13 CDS Public Data (Brief)

Index CDS (CFTC swap repositories) and, since early 2022, single-name CDS (SEC Regulation SBSR; *date approximate*) have public tapes, with capped sizes and painful entity mapping. Use them for activity and basis signals (Chapter 24) and buy levels from a vendor.

## B.14 Open-Source Tooling

| Tool | What it does | Verified notes (2026-10-17) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `edgartools` (<https://github.com/dgunning/edgartools>) | EDGAR filings, XBRL statements, full-text search | MIT; Python 3.11+; call `set_identity("name@example.com")` first; stays within 10 req/s |
| OpenBB Open Data Platform (<https://github.com/OpenBB-finance/OpenBB>) | One data layer for public and licensed providers (Python, REST, MCP) | `pip install openbb`; Apache-2.0; Python 3.10–3.14; `openbb-api` serves on port 6900 |
| `pandas-datareader` (<https://pandas-datareader.readthedocs.io/en/latest/>) | Remote readers, including FRED | 0.11.2 dev build in the docs (July 2026); FRED now returns 3 years for ICE series |
| `juriscraper` | Court and PACER parsing | BSD-2; Python 3.11+ |
| trace-data-pipeline / PyBondLab | TRACE cleaning, analytics, factors | MIT; Stages 0–1 need WRDS |

> **Ways This Blows Up.** When a provider changes its terms (FRED's window, CourtListener's limits, EDGAR's User-Agent rule), the wrappers break *quietly*. A call that returns three years of OAS where it used to return thirty raises no exception. It just deletes 2008 from your regime model. Assert row counts and date ranges on every pull, and fail the job if history shrinks.

## B.15 Case Study: A Fallen Angel Through Every Lens

Take the synthetic `SYN-IG-B` from the code below (all numbers *illustrative*). Its downgrade from BBB- to BB+ takes effect June 10 and is published June 12. TRACE prints switch from `5MM+` to `1MM+` on June 12. Join on effective date and you "know" the cap change two days early. The index keeps the bond until the June month-end rebalance, which is when forced selling clusters. Composites mark it down slowly, at high $\theta$, so composite-based daily returns understate the move's volatility. A Dimson-summed beta to HYG recovers it.

The desk's job is to line these five clocks up by `knowledge_ts`. That alignment is a feature in its own right. The gap between the downgrade's knowledge time and the index rebalance is the forced-selling window that Chapters 9 and 20 trade.

## B.16 Specification for AI Implementation: The Tidy Bond Panel

**The Spec You Hand the Robot.** *What ROBO built from the vague version ("make me a daily bond price table"):* it took the last trade of each day and forward-filled across holidays and weekends. It dropped the defaulted bond because its yield failed to solve. It joined ratings on effective date. Every one of those choices ships a bias into production. Here is the precise version.

| Table | Key | Required columns (units) | Rules |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `secmaster` | `bond_id` | coupon (decimal), maturity, offering_amt (\$ par), security_level, rule_144a, freq, day_count | One row per bond; IDs are synthetic in tests, CUSIPs in production (licensed) |
| `ratings` | (`bond_id`, `knowledge_ts`) | effective_ts, knowledge_ts, rating, rating_num (1 = AAA … 22 = D) | As-of join on `knowledge_ts` only |
| `msgs` | `msg_seq` | trc_st ∈ {T, X, C}, orig_msg_seq, exec_ts, report_ts, price (% of par), qty_true (\$ par), side ∈ {B, S, D} | Simplified status codes; map FINRA's real codes per vintage (pre/post 2012) |
| `trades` | `msg_seq` | + rating at trade, cap, qty_dissem, qty_capped, flags | No cancelled or corrected originals; screens for decimal shifts and bounce-backs |
| `daily` | (`bond_id`, `date`) | px_clean, px_vwap_dissem, n_trades, par_volume, days_stale, is_stale, status, accrued, ytm, dur_mod, spread (decimal), dts (yr·bp) | Full business-day grid until maturity; defaulted bonds kept, flagged `trades_flat` |
| `monthly` | (`bond_id`, `month_end`) | px_eom, accrued, cpn_paid, ret_total | Month-end price only if `days_stale` ≤ 5; else NaN, never filled |

Edge cases the code must handle: settlement on T+1 business day; 30/360 accrual to settlement; flat trading (zero accrued, no yield) after default; caps keyed to point-in-time rating; Brent bracket of $[-5\%, 500\%]$ for distressed yields. Sanity checks: price–yield round trip to $10^{-8}$; analytic vs. finite-difference duration to $10^{-6}$; a par bond priced on a coupon date equals 100; and a Monte Carlo check of the §B.0 result $\operatorname{Var}(r^o)/\sigma^2=(1-\theta)/(1+\theta)$, $\rho_1=\theta$. The spread is a curve-interpolated G-spread against an *illustrative* Nelson–Siegel curve, not OAS. Requires pandas ≥ 2.2.

## B.17 Desk Debrief

- **Every price has a clock.** Store `exec_ts`, `report_ts`, and `knowledge_ts` separately, and join only on knowledge.
- **Staleness hides risk; it doesn't remove it.** Observed variance shrinks by $(1-\theta)/(1+\theta)$, and summing lagged betas brings the full beta back.
- **The public TRACE tape is censored** at \$5mm IG and \$1mm HY. The cap follows the bond's point-in-time rating.
- **The 15-minute window survived.** One-minute reporting was approved in 2024 and abandoned in 2025, for both TRACE and the MSRB.
- **EDGAR misses the 10% hole, the redactions, and every 144A-for-life issuer.** Your covenant model has a coverage map whether you draw it or not.
- **Free data shrinks.** FRED's ICE series now keep 3 years and CourtListener allows 125 requests a day by default. Cache, version, and assert row counts.
- **Composites are model outputs.** Validate against later trades, never against themselves.
- **IDO or it didn't happen**, and IDO on stale prices didn't happen either.

**The Spec You Hand the Robot (summary).** "Build `daily` on a full business-day grid per bond until maturity. Never drop defaulted bonds; flag them `trades_flat`. Clean messages by matching X and C records to originals by `orig_msg_seq`. Join ratings by `merge_asof` on `knowledge_ts` and assert there is no look-ahead. Compute caps from point-in-time ratings. Carry prices forward only with an explicit `days_stale`, and leave a month-end return as NaN when `days_stale` > 5. Enforce dtypes by kind, keep keys unique, and pass the price–yield, duration, par, and staleness checks, or fail the build."

**Exercises.**
1. Estimate $\theta$ for each bond in `daily` from $\rho_1$ of returns on days with trades. Compare it with the variance-ratio estimate. Which one is more robust when trading days are irregular?
2. Fit a Pareto tail to `qty_true` above \$1mm for HY prints. Impute sizes for `1MM+` prints and measure the bias you remove from a capped VWAP.
3. Using the EDGAR full-text syntax, write a query for 8-K exhibits that pair "unrestricted subsidiary" with "intellectual property," and list three ways it gives false positives.

### Deep-Dive Resource Graph

**Podcasts.** Bloomberg's *Odd Lots* (bond market-structure episodes); *Flirting with Models* (Corey Hoffstein).

**Practitioner Writing.** Matt Levine, *Money Stuff* (on bond-market transparency and the "price" of untraded bonds); MarketAxess TraX and CP+ research; Free Law Project's CourtListener documentation (<https://wiki.free.law/c/courtlistener/help/api/rest/v4/overview>).

**Academic Papers.** Dick-Nielsen (2009), *Liquidity Biases in TRACE*; Dick-Nielsen (2014), *How to Clean Enhanced TRACE Data*; Dimson (1979), *Risk Measurement When Shares Are Subject to Infrequent Trading*; Getmansky, Lo & Makarov (2004), *An Econometric Model of Serial Correlation and Illiquidity in Hedge Fund Returns*; Edwards, Harris & Piwowar (2007), *Corporate Bond Market Transaction Costs and Transparency*; Bessembinder, Kahle, Maxwell & Xu (2009), *Measuring Abnormal Bond Performance*; Bai, Bali & Wen (2019), *Common Risk Factors in the Cross-Section of Corporate Bond Returns*; Dickerson, Mueller & Robotti (2023), *Priced Risk in Corporate Bonds*; Dickerson, Robotti & Rossetti, *The Corporate Bond Factor Replication Crisis* (working paper).

**Data & Code.** FINRA TRACE historic data (<https://www.finra.org/filing-reporting/trace/historic-academic-data>); SEC EDGAR APIs (<https://www.sec.gov/edgar/sec-api-documentation>); RECAP Fetch (<https://wiki.free.law/c/courtlistener/help/api/rest/v4/recap>); FRED HY OAS (<https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/BAMLH0A0HYM2>); OBAP pipeline (<https://github.com/Alexander-M-Dickerson/trace-data-pipeline>); edgartools (<https://github.com/dgunning/edgartools>); OpenBB (<https://github.com/OpenBB-finance/OpenBB>). # Appendix C: The Trend Tracker

## C.0 Why Trends Are the Spine

The corridor outside the systematic credit desk has been taken over by paper. Theo Marsh has printed all 74 Trend Watch boxes in this book, cut out every dated line, and taped them to the wall in order. The strip starts with a fax machine and ends, eleven meters later, with an AI agent that still fails about one structured task in three.

"It's one story," Theo says. "Twenty-eight chapters, and every box answers the same three questions: what changed, when, and how big. The book has a spine, and I'm looking at it."

"Two spines," says Kaz Lind. "One is structural trends. E-share goes up, recoveries go down, default turns into a negotiation. Those move over years, and you use them to decide what to build. The other is trend-following, Chapter 10: prices that keep going the way they were going. Those move over months, and you use them to decide what to hold." Kaz squints at the 2026 end of the strip. "I assume a 'drop-down' is the same in both. A menu."

"It is a menu," says Mags Dunleavy. "Of assets, sorted by how fast they leave the collateral package. Back in my day you found out about a trend from the recovery, three years late, in the lawyers' invoice. This one has dates and sources. I'll allow it."

Ines Okafor is reading the 2025 section. "Same game at two speeds. A structural trend is a hand that takes eight years to play out. A price trend takes eight months. Either way the question is whether you're early, late, or the player everyone else is reading. And half of these numbers disagree with each other."

"So there's a section for that," Theo says.

ROBO, asked to "track the trends," has computed a 12-month moving average of the word *trend* across the manuscript. The series is rising. ROBO is not wrong.

This appendix is the wall, cleaned up. §C.1 boils the 74 boxes down to seven megatrends. Each one gets a thesis, its key numbers, the chapters it feeds, and the indicators to watch in 2027. §C.2 is the master timeline: one row per sourced fact, deduplicated across chapters. §C.3 collects the numbers on which good sources disagree, and explains why. §C.4 tells the next edition's editor how to keep the tracker alive. Everything here comes from the Trend Watch boxes and the research notes behind them, compiled on 2026-10-18. The appendix adds no new research, so it inherits every *approx.* and every CHECK flag from its sources.

## C.1 The Seven Megatrends of Credit, 2018–2026

A megatrend is a direction that showed up in at least three chapters and in more than one independent data series. It is not a forecast. The seven overlap on purpose. Megatrends 1, 2 and 3 are the same machine seen from the trader's seat, the product shelf and the regulator's desk. Megatrends 4 and 5 are one capital structure seen before and after the lawyers.

| # | Megatrend | One-line thesis | Main chapters |
| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |
| 1 | The quote went electronic, then automatic | Machines answer the small tickets; adverse selection concentrates in what is left | 1, 2, 3, 4, 18, 27 |
| 2 | Risk moves in baskets | PT, ETFs, index CDS and futures carry more risk than single bonds | 2, 8, 10, 19, 20, 24 |
| 3 | The dealer became a router, and the tape was re-plumbed | Inventory left the banks; the meaning of a TRACE print changes yearly | 2, 18, 22, 27 |
| 4 | Default became a negotiation | The distressed exchange is the modal default, and re-default is the base case | 3, 5, 6, 13, 14, 16 |
| 5 | The cushion and the covenants disappeared | Recoveries compress, covenants vanish, and the CCC tier decouples | 5, 8, 11, 12, 25 |
| 6 | Leverage moved off the public tape | Loans, CLOs and private credit grew; public HY stood still | 1, 12, 17, 21 |
| 7 | Quant credit grew up | Bought rather than built, audited, automated, and trend-tested | 4, 7, 9, 10, 26 |

### C.1.1 Megatrend 1: The Quote Went Electronic, Then Automatic

*Thesis.* Between 2018 and 2026, US corporate bonds moved from voice to venues, and then from venues to machines. By at least one definition IG crossed the halfway line; HY has stalled near a third. The share is not the deep change. The deep change is who answers. The small, uninformed ticket now gets an algorithm's reply in milliseconds at close to the minimum spread. Adverse selection did not go away. It moved into the large, stressed, event-adjacent tickets that are still left for humans, which is the ex-RSSG reader's home game. Automation is also a fair-weather technology. The robots widen their parameters or switch off when the market gaps, so the stress cost of liquidity has not fallen the way the calm-market cost has.

*Key numbers.* IG e-share was 20% in 2015, 48% in 2024 and 52% in June 2025; HY was 6% in 2015, then 33% in 2024 and 32% in 2025 (Coalition Greenwich). ADNV rose from \$46.2bn (2024) to more than \$50bn (2025) to \$61bn (January 2026), and daily turnover went from 0.33% of outstanding (2021) to 0.44% (2024). About 30% of dealer volume ran with no human touch in June 2024. Tradeweb's AiEX handled more than 40% of its institutional trades in 2025 (30% in 2021), Trumid ran 88% of eligible RFQ line items fully no-touch in September 2025, and Vanguard automated about 70% of its desk volume by October 2026. Non-bank liquidity providers earned about 10% of US credit market-making revenue in 2024. In the March 2026 stress, EUR IG bid–ask hit 64% above its January average, and recovery took between 4 weeks (EUR IG) and 14+ weeks (EM).

*Feeds.* Chapters 1, 2, 3, 4, 11, 18, 19 and 27.

*Watch in 2027.* Whether HY breaks out of the 30–33% band on Greenwich's annual series. No-touch share and auto-execution fill rates on high-VIX days, which is the "auto-ex stops executing" signal. The non-bank share of market-making revenue, which Coalition Greenwich expects to grow over the next two to three years. Bid–ask recovery half-life after the next shock. The ICE–MarketAxess closing, expected in H1 2027, and whether the market leader's monthly volume data come back.

### C.1.2 Megatrend 2: Risk Moves in Baskets

*Thesis.* Credit risk increasingly changes hands as a basket rather than as a bond. Portfolio trading went from a curiosity to standard plumbing. Bond ETFs went from a side door to a main entrance. Index CDS absorbed the derivatives market while single-name CDS thinned out, and listed credit futures arrived in 2024. The resulting triangle (ETF, portfolio trade, cash) is regime-dependent. In calm markets, PT does the risk transfer and the ETF share of volume falls. In stress, the ETF is again the only instrument that trades at size. Basket flow also clusters at the index mark, so time of day is now a cost variable.

*Key numbers.* PT was about 1% of IG volume in 2018, 7% in 2021, and 10% of IG and 8% of HY in 2024. It was 18% of the \$84.7bn record day on 30 September 2025 and 19.8% of customer volume in Q1 2026, when 15.5% of all corporate volume printed at the index mark (5% in 2016). US bond ETFs held \$1.8tn at end-2024, 17% of all ETF assets, while the ETF-to-cash volume ratio fell from 23.2% (2022) to 16.6% (2024). Then \$99bn of fixed-income ETFs traded on 7 April 2025. CDS trading set a record \$41.8tn in 2025, of which index products were 93.3%; single-name activity fell from its 2023 peak of \$3.3tn to \$2.8tn. Only 20 of 751 single-name reference entities averaged ten or more trades a day in Q4 2025. Cboe iBoxx credit-futures blocks topped \$1bn a month in July and August 2026. US CLO ETFs passed \$50bn in July 2026.

*Feeds.* Chapters 2, 8, 10, 19, 20, 21 and 24.

*Watch in 2027.* PT share on each denominator, labeled. Bondwave's index-mark share. The ETF discount and the ETF-to-cash ratio as a stress detector. Credit-futures open interest and block counts, now that IBIG blocks have overtaken IBHY. ISDA's single-name breadth. CLO ETF flows, which are effectively a bid for CLO resets.

### C.1.3 Megatrend 3: The Dealer Became a Router, and the Tape Was Re-plumbed

*Thesis.* Bank dealers stopped warehousing corporate bonds. By 2026 the street was net short on average, which Coalition Greenwich's analysis says had not happened in at least 25 years. The inventory function moved to customers: all-to-all venues, ETF creation and redemption, and portfolio trades. Meanwhile the public tape changed its definitions about once a year. The PT modifier came in 2023 and T+1 in 2024. A one-minute reporting rule was approved and then abandoned. Optional aggregate allocation reports began in 2026, and an affiliate-print flag phases in during 2026–27. Treasury clearing is moving the financing of a bond book onto cleared, margined, netted rails. None of these dates changed the economic volume. All of them changed what a print means.

*Key numbers.* Dealers held about \$235bn of corporates at the 2007 peak (approx.; upper bound), averaged about \$16bn long in 2017, and were about \$4bn net short on average in 2026 (approx.). FINRA's statistics show 82.9% of 2022 trades already reported within one minute. Duplicate affiliate prints inflated high-grade TRACE volume by up to 8% in June 2026. FICC cleared a peak of \$11.8trn on 30 June 2025 (approx.). Open Trading carried 35.2%, 35.0% and 37.0% of eligible MarketAxess volume over 2023–2025, so all-to-all is a structural minority, not a takeover.

*Feeds.* Chapters 2, 18, 22 and 27, and Appendix B.

*Watch in 2027.* The mandatory affiliate indicator on 2 August 2027, after which volume series de-inflate. Treasury cash clearing on 31 December 2026 and repo on 30 June 2027, each with a placebo twin in case it slips. Whether the net short in the NY Fed primary-dealer statistics persists. N-PORT's move to quarterly reporting from November 2027.

### C.1.4 Megatrend 4: Default Became a Negotiation

*Thesis.* The modal default is now a distressed exchange, timed by lender calls and documents rather than by a missed coupon. LMT counts peaked at 38 in 2024 and fell to 24 in 2025, but the soft share of defaults did not fall. The technique migrated from coercive uptiers to amend-extend-and-exchange, drop-downs, deals away and equity handovers. The courts made outcomes depend on contract tokens: "open market purchase" in *Serta*, a bare "purchase" in Mitel. The creditor counter-technology, the cooperation agreement, went from a rarity to a default setting and then to an antitrust defendant. Re-default is the base case, and it is front-loaded.

*Key numbers.* Distressed exchanges were about 32% of S&P-rated defaults in 2010–2023, about half for three years to mid-2024, about 63% of Moody's-rated defaults in 2024, about 65% in 2025, and "roughly 70%" since early 2022 (Moody's, September 2026). In June 2025 the spec-grade default rate was 5.8% including distressed exchanges and 2.1% excluding them. About 45 co-ops were signed in 2024, against about four a year over 2018–2023. (Cooperation agreements signed in this book so far: still fewer than the US signed in 2024.) Of 1,173 soft-event borrowers since 1979, about one in four hard-defaulted, more than 70% of them within two years. About 46% of 2023 distressed exchanges had re-defaulted by April 2025, and only 22% of 89 coercive LMEs were clean after two years. Before 2020, about 40% of loans restricted uptiers; by mid-2022, 85% of new loans blocked them.

*Feeds.* Chapters 1, 3, 5, 6, 11, 13, 14, 16 and 25.

*Watch in 2027.* The gap between headline and ex-DE default rates, a regime variable in its own right (§14.7). The 2024 cohort of 38 LMTs crossing the two-year re-default window. The Optimum co-op antitrust case in the S.D.N.Y. and Optimum's April and July 2027 maturities. Fifth Circuit appeals in Wesco and *ConvergeOne*. The \$580bn loan and \$625bn HY maturity wall over 2027–2029. Company adviser hires, which lead LMTs by months.

### C.1.5 Megatrend 5: The Cushion and the Covenants Disappeared

*Thesis.* Leveraged capital structures lost their junior debt cushion and their maintenance covenants at the same time. First-lien recoveries migrated down as structures became first-lien-heavy, and the early-warning device that used to give lenders a seat at the table, the covenant trip, was replaced by incurrence baskets that only tell you what the borrower is allowed to do next. Recovery became bimodal, conditional on whether you were inside the deal. The bottom of the high-yield stack then came apart from the top: by October 2026 the CCC tier priced its widest levels of the window while BBs sat near their tights, and the index spread looked calm.

*Key numbers.* Long-run first-lien term-loan ultimate recovery was 71% over 1987–2023, but S&P's first-lien recovery ratings had fallen to the mid-to-low 60s by February 2025, against realized averages of 75–80%, and Moody's projected first-lien loan recoveries "declining to 55%" (September 2026). First-lien and priority debt now exceed 75% of typical structures. Cov-lite loans were 88.91% of outstanding US leveraged loans at year-end 2022 and 91.09% at year-end 2024. The share of public firms reporting a covenant violation fell from over 12% (1997) to under 5% (2016). The CCC-and-lower OAS went from 746bp (end-2024) to 885bp (end-2025) to 1,278bp (15 October 2026), while BB went 186, 169, 197bp; the CCC/BB ratio rose from 4.0× to 5.2× to 6.5×. CCC beta to HY spread changes fell from 0.54 (2024) to 0.45 (2026 YTD). On the Serta remand, the excluded loans were valued at 25 cents.

*Feeds.* Chapters 5, 8, 11, 12, 14, 16 and 25.

*Watch in 2027.* The CCC/HY OAS ratio as a mixture-weight indicator (Chapter 12). Moody's annual default-and-recovery study, and whether first-lien recoveries really print near 55%. The full-year 2025 cov-lite figure, which was not verified for this edition. Software concentration in loan and private-credit books. Refits of the debt-cushion and loan-only coefficients in the recovery model on post-2019 defaults.

### C.1.6 Megatrend 6: Leverage Moved Off the Public Tape

*Thesis.* Public high yield stopped growing and got better rated. The growth in leveraged finance went to institutional loans, mostly owned by rule-bound CLOs, and to private credit, mostly marked by models. More of the market now sits with holders whose sales are triggered by rules (CLO tests, NAIC capital charges, ETF flows, 5% redemption gates) and less with dealers whose balance sheets used to absorb them. Private credit's failure mode shifted from defaults to redemptions, and its first redemption cycle arrived in Q1 2026. At the same time it began building public-market plumbing (daily pricing, identifiers, official statistics), which turns marks into prices and makes the gap between them tradable.

*Key numbers.* The HY index had about \$1.4tn of face value in April 2025, essentially unchanged over ten years, with a BB share of 53.55% against a 1996–2024 average of 44.53%. Institutional leveraged loans reached \$1,549bn at 2025:Q4. CLOs hold about two-thirds of the loan market and buy "nearly three-quarters" of new issue, yet 2025's roughly \$400bn of gross loan issuance produced only about \$106bn of net new loans. Private-credit loans on the Fed's new Z.1 basis were \$1,042.6bn (2023), \$1,253.6bn (2024) and \$1,493.5bn (2025). Semi-liquid fund net assets went from about \$15bn (2018) to \$388bn (2025). In Q1 2026, accepted redemptions exceeded inflows for the first time since those vehicles were created. Bank loans are about 40% of BDC debt, double their share a decade earlier. Life insurers' privately placed bonds reached 48.4% of their bond holdings at YE2025 (see §C.3 on the competing measure).

*Feeds.* Chapters 1, 12, 16, 17 and 21.

*Watch in 2027.* The quarterly Z.1 private-credit series. Semi-liquid redemption requests against the 5% caps, and the dispersion (not the mean) of listed BDC discounts. Private-credit default measures with PIK and extensions included. NAIC's CLO C-1 factors, effective with YE2026 RBC. The share of loans priced above par, which says whether the repricing window is open. Octaura's share of secondary loan volume (7.5–7.7% in H1 2026).

### C.1.7 Megatrend 7: Quant Credit Grew Up

*Thesis.* The plumbing for systematic credit scaled faster than the capital dedicated to it. Pure systematic credit is still under 2% of the investable fixed-income universe, against about 20% of equities. The money went to hybrids (quant screens feeding analysts) and to large platforms that bought an engine rather than built one. The academic foundation was audited, and much of the corporate-bond factor zoo did not survive cleaned data. ML research moved from "can it predict?" to "can we trust the inputs?" to "can the model explain itself?" AI made reading cheap and left checking expensive. Trend-following, the book's second spine, turned out to be an index strategy in credit. It is small and slow, it sits inside crowded CTA books, and since 2024 it has faced a high-yield spread band too narrow to clear the carry hurdle.

*Key numbers.* Actively managed quant credit was about \$52bn in 2021, and quant-screened IG and HY funds were \$90–140bn in 2024. At Man Group, systematic long-only credit went from \$2.0bn (March 2025) to \$3.1bn (September 2026), while discretionary long-only credit went from \$19.8bn to \$37.5bn. Blackstone agreed to buy DCI in 2020, and Ares agreed to buy BlueCove in October 2025. In the 2026 replication audit, 26 of 432 specifications (6.0%) survived a false-discovery correction. Robeco's live multi-factor credit fund returned 0.63% a year since its 2015 inception against 0.87% for its benchmark (to September 2026). The inference cost of GPT-3.5-level performance fell more than 280-fold between November 2022 and October 2024, while 2,199 court decisions involving hallucinated content had been logged by October 2026. The SG Trend Index made +27.3% in 2022, drew down −21.8% from April 2024 to May 2025, and stood +11.07% YTD at end-August 2026. Pairwise correlation among its constituents was 0.78 in 2024. HY OAS spent 2024–2026 between 2.59% and 4.61%.

*Feeds.* Chapters 1, 4, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 23 and 26.

*Watch in 2027.* Man Group's quarterly systematic-versus-discretionary split, the cleanest public flow series. Systematic-credit M&A, with Ares–BlueCove as the template. The outcome of the replication paper's revision and the next Open Source Bond Asset Pricing release. IGEB and HYDB assets. CTA crowding (pairwise correlation and same-direction drawdowns). Whether HY OAS breaks out of its 2024–2026 band for long enough to give credit trend something to follow.

Three causes explain nearly every row: *definition* (what counts as electronic, a default, or an LMT), *denominator* (TRACE, customer volume, or institutional trades), and *vintage* (which year's capital structure, which revision of the chart). The desk rule from Chapter 2 applies to the whole table. Never average two contested figures. Carry both, label each with its definition, and let the model choose the one that matches its own target variable. Ines's version: "When two honest sources disagree, you've learned something about the deck, not about the dealer."

## C.4 How to Update This Appendix

The tracker is a dated object, and its value decays at the speed of the trends it tracks. For the next edition:

1. **Start from the watch lists.** Each megatrend's "Watch in 2027" list is the first update target. Score every indicator as *moved as expected*, *flat*, or *reversed*, and keep that scorecard in the appendix. A tracker that never admits it was wrong is just a brochure.
2. **One fact, one row.** Search the timeline before adding a row. If the event is already there, add your chapter number to it. The earliest dated primary source wins the Source column; later citations go in the chapters.
3. **Date the event, not the article.** Put the publication date in the Source column, and follow the sorting rules at the top of §C.2.
4. **Source or delete.** Name the document. Write "via" for secondary reporting. Add a URL only if it was verified in that session or is a canonical root.
5. **Expire the flags.** An *approx.* or CHECK that survives two editions is resolved against the primary source or deleted. It is not inherited a third time.
6. **Log the breaks.** When a reporting rule changes (the 2027-08-02 affiliate indicator, the N-PORT move to quarterly reporting), add a timeline row *and* a regime tag in Appendix B, so that no series silently changes meaning.
7. **Contested means unreconciled.** A pair joins §C.3 only after the definitions have been checked, and it leaves once someone has reconciled it.
8. **Re-cut the seven.** Retire a megatrend once it stops producing new rows. Promote a candidate once it appears in three chapters and two independent series.

> **The Spec You Hand the Robot.** *What ROBO built from the vague version ("keep the tracker up to date"):* a nightly job that sets every date to today. *The spec:* maintain `trend_tracker.csv` with columns `date` (ISO; plus `date_precision` ∈ {day, month, quarter, year}), `event`, `magnitude`, `unit`, `source`, `source_type` ∈ {primary, secondary}, `approx` (bool), `check` (bool), `chapters` (list of ints), `megatrend` ∈ {1, …, 7}, and `last_verified` (ISO). The sort key follows §C.2. Reject any row with an empty `source`. Raise a warning when `check` is true and `last_verified` is more than 365 days old. Flag two rows as duplicates when they share `event`, `date` and `magnitude`. Never edit `date` on an existing row: corrections go in a new row that names the one it supersedes.

# Appendix D: Plumbing: Settlement, Clearing, Margin, Financing and the ISDA Credit-Event Machine

## D.0 Cold Open: Hedged on the P&L, Naked on the Wire

*Tuesday, 4:52 p.m.* The sticky-note trade from Chapter 24 had gone through on Monday: \$10mm Halvorsen Packaging 6% 2031 at 88, and \$10mm of five-year Halvorsen protection. (Halvorsen is fictional; all numbers illustrative.) The risk system showed the package as flat. The operations queue showed four lines in red.

*Halvorsen 6% 2031: FAIL. Counterparty short, chain fail.* *Repo: unfunded, collateral not received.* *CDS: initial margin call, \$600,000, posted 09:02.* *Larkspur Foam 2029 TLB: pending agent consent, day 12.*

"The trade is hedged," Theo said. "Why is my screen red?"

"Because the hedge lives on the P&L," Ines said, "and the queue lives on the wire. Different tables, different chips. The P&L tells you what you'll have. The wire tells you whether you'll still be seated when you get it."

"It's a timing difference," said Kaz. "In expectation it's zero."

"So is a margin call you can't meet," said Mags, "for about a day." She did not look up. "Back in my day a fail meant a messenger with a bag of certificates who got lost on Water Street. At least you knew where the bond was. It was in the bag."

Kaz brightened. "Wait, if the seller failed to deliver, is that a Failure to Pay? Do we trigger the swap?"

"A fail is when the bond doesn't show up," Mags said. "Failure to Pay is when the coupon doesn't. One costs the seller a day's interest. The other costs somebody par minus recovery. Please never ask that in front of a Determinations Committee."

Theo had told ROBO on Friday to "make sure everything settles." ROBO did exactly that: it set every settlement date equal to the trade date. The backtest P&L was perfect, and the bank account was not.

**Between the handshake and the money, who holds what, for how long, against how much collateral, and what does a contract mean by "default" when the money does not arrive?**

By the end of this appendix you will be able to: read the settlement calendar of every instrument the book trades and price a fail or a settlement gap; tell initial margin from variation margin and compute a netted margin; turn a repo haircut into leverage, return on equity and a forced-selling schedule; name the funding leg of every basis in the book; compute a CDS's day-one cash, including the upfront and the accrued rebate; walk a credit event from the missed coupon to the auction's final price; and check a deliverable, a successor and an orphan against the rules.

**How to use this appendix.** It is a reference, so it is mostly tables. The derivations already live elsewhere: settlement clocks and clearing economics in §22.3–22.6, loan settlement in §21.2, ETF settlement gaps in §20.6, and CDS legs, funding, cheapest-to-deliver, the auction and succession in §24.2 and §24.4–24.8. This appendix gives each mechanism one table and one formula, with a back-reference to its derivation. Each section ends with a **Used in:** line so you can go from a term to the places it matters.

> **Prerequisites.** Clean and dirty prices and day counts (Chapter 4-B; App A §A.4); the risky annuity RPV01 and the credit triangle (§6.8); the two legs of a CDS (§24.2).

*Notation.* In this appendix a roman T+k is a settlement offset of $k$ business days after trade date. An italic $t+1$ is still the next period of a time series, as App A §A.3 resolves that collision. The haircut is $h$, the repo funding spread is $\phi$, and repo specialness is $\ell$, as in §24.4. The margin period of risk is $H$ (in days), as in (22.8). Where Chapter 22's netting factor appears, it is written $\phi^{\text{net}}$ so that it cannot be confused with the funding spread.

**Used in:** Chapter 24's cold open (the same trade, priced); §D.8 (the same trade, through the pipes); App E (the Law numbers that tag §D.10).

## D.1 The Settlement Clock: Four Instruments, Four Calendars

A trade is two promises with a gap between them. At T you agree a price; at T+k one side delivers the asset and the other delivers the cash. In between, each side is exposed to the other's failure to perform, which costs the price move since T if the counterparty disappears and a day of interest if it is merely late. Clearing houses margin the first risk (§D.2). Market convention prices the second. Everything else in this section is a calendar.

**Table D.1. Settlement cycles and fail regimes (US unless stated; simplified).**

| Instrument | Convention | What actually happens | Ledger and rails | If it fails | Built in |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| US Treasuries | T+1 (market convention; T+0 common) | Same day for many dealer trades | Fedwire Securities; FICC nets members' trades | TMPG fails charge, so the cost of failing is $\max(r^{\text{ref}}, 3\%)$, eq. (22.9) | §22.3.2, §22.4 |
| US corporate bonds (IG, HY, 144A) | T+1 since 2024-05-28 (T+2 from 2017-09-05, T+3 before) | New issues often settle on a longer, expressly agreed cycle *(approx.)* | DTC book entry; NSCC compares and nets eligible trades | Seller loses the use of the cash; the buyer's remedy is a buy-in under the FINRA Uniform Practice Code (Rule 11810; check the current text) | §22.3 |
| European corporate bonds | T+2; T+1 from 2027-10-11 | The UK targets the same date | Euroclear, Clearstream, T2S | CSDR cash penalties per day of fail (since 2022-02-01); mandatory buy-ins not in force | Trend Watch, §D.7 |
| Par leveraged loans (LSTA) | T+7, with delayed compensation after T+7 | Average about 20 business days *(approx.; §21.2.1)* | Agent bank's register; assignment agreement; ClearPar | No fail as such; delayed compensation shifts the carry (§21.2.2) | §21.2 |
| Distressed loans (LSTA) | T+20 | Months are not unusual; Moyer reports up to 120 days in 2004 | Agent register; purchase-and-sale agreement with the upstream chain | Settlement risk on the chain of prior sellers | §21.2.1 |
| Single-name CDS and CDX/iTraxx | Step-in T+1 (calendar); upfront cash T+3 business days | No principal changes hands | CCP (ICE Clear Credit, LCH CDSClear) or bilateral under an ISDA/CSA; DTCC Trade Information Warehouse | Nothing to fail: margin calls instead (§D.2) | §24.2, §D.4 |
| Credit ETF shares (HYG, JNK, LQD, BKLN) | T+1 | Secondary trades settle like equities | NSCC CNS, DTC | CNS fail; equity close-out rules apply to short sales | Ch 20 |
| ETF primary market (create, redeem) | Generally T+1, matching the shares | In-kind bond baskets settle T+1; loan funds deliver or raise cash on loan timelines | AP and fund agent; custom baskets | The fund or AP finances the gap | §20.1, §20.6.1 |
| Listed credit futures | Daily variation margin; final cash settlement | | CME, Cboe, ICE and Eurex clearing | Margin default, not a fail | Ch 10-B |
| Repo | T+0 or T+1 start; overnight or term | Mostly overnight | Tri-party (BNY), bilateral, FICC sponsored | Treasury fails charge on the collateral leg | §D.3 |
| Bankruptcy trade claims | No convention | Weeks; transfer is noticed under Bankruptcy Rule 3001(e) | Claims agent's register | Objection risk, not a fail | Ch 12-B, §16.5 |

**The cash at settlement.** Bonds are quoted clean and settle dirty, with accrued interest counted to the *settlement* date, not the trade date. For face $N$, clean price $P^{\text{clean}}$ in points and an annual coupon $c$ on 30/360:

$$
\text{Cash}_{\text{settle}} = N\left(\frac{P^{\text{clean}}}{100} + c\,\frac{d_{30/360}\big(t_{\text{cpn}^-},\,t_{\text{settle}}\big)}{360}\right),
$$

where $t_{\text{cpn}^-}$ is the last coupon date. The invoice is fixed at the *contractual* settlement date. If the seller fails, the buyer pays the same invoice later, so the seller bears the cost of the delay: the interest on the cash it has not received, $\text{Cash}_{\text{settle}}\cdot r^{\text{ref}}\cdot d^{\text{fail}}/360$, plus any penalty. In Treasuries the TMPG charge puts a floor of 3% a year under that cost, eq. (22.9). In US corporates there is no charge, so the discipline comes from buy-ins and from the counterparty's memory.

**The settlement gap.** When two legs of one position settle $\Delta d$ days apart, somebody finances the cash for the difference:

$$
C^{\text{gap}} = \text{Cash}\cdot r^{\text{fund}}\cdot\frac{\Delta d}{360}.
$$

A loan fund that owes redemption cash at T+1 against loans whose sale settles in about 20 business days (call it 28 calendar days) finances \$100mm for 27 days. At a 5% funding rate that is about \$375,000 *(illustrative)*, or 38 bp of the redemption, paid by the holders who stay. That is §20.6.1's "basket that cannot settle" in one line. The gap is also why ROBO's cold-open shortcut fails: setting every settlement date equal to the trade date silently books $C^{\text{gap}} = 0$ on every trade.

> **Ways This Blows Up.** (1) *Holiday calendars.* The bond market follows SIFMA's calendar, not the stock exchange's: SIFMA recommends a full close on Columbus Day and Veterans Day while the NYSE is open, so a T+1 bond trade done the Friday before Columbus Day settles on Tuesday, while a T+1 ETF trade settles on Monday. A basket trade that mixes the two has a one-day settlement gap built into the calendar. (2) *Accrued to the wrong date.* Accruing to trade date rather than settlement date is one day of coupon on every trade; across a 150-line portfolio trade it is a systematic P&L leak, and it is invisible in a backtest that never settles. (3) *Treating "T+7" as a date.* For loans it is the day delayed compensation starts, not the day cash moves; model the settlement lag as a random variable (§21.2.2), not a constant.

**Used in:** Chapter 4-B (clean, dirty, day counts); §20.1 and §20.6.1 (ETF settlement and the loan-fund gap); §21.2.1–21.2.2 (loan settlement, delayed compensation); §22.3 (T+1 and fails); App A §A.4 (day-count table).

## D.2 Clearing, Netting and the Two Margins

A central counterparty (CCP) steps between buyer and seller by *novation*: the original trade is replaced by two trades, each against the CCP. The CCP then nets each member's trades into one position and asks for two kinds of collateral. "It's the only player at the table who never bluffs and never leaves," Ines says. "It just makes everyone post a stack before the cards come out, and it counts the stack again every night."

**Variation margin (VM)** settles the day's mark-to-market in cash: $\text{VM}_t = V_t - V_{t-1}$, paid by the loser to the winner, usually the next morning. Across the market VM sums to zero. CCPs credit or charge interest on accumulated VM (price alignment interest) so that a cleared trade's economics match an uncleared one's. **Initial margin (IM)** covers the loss the CCP could suffer between a member's default and the close-out of its book, the margin period of risk $H$. In the square-root form of §22.3.1, for a position $x$ with daily volatility $\sigma$,

$$
\text{IM} = z_\alpha\,\sigma\sqrt{H}\,|x|.
$$

VM is a transfer and IM is a tax on the horizon. A hedged book pays almost no net VM, but it still posts IM on any risk that does not net, and IM is funded at the desk's funding spread $f$.

**Netting, derived.** For a book of positions $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with daily covariance $\Sigma$, portfolio IM is $z_\alpha\sqrt{H}\sqrt{x^\top\Sigma x}$, against a gross sum of standalone margins $z_\alpha\sqrt{H}\sum_i\sigma_i|x_i|$. Take $n$ equal long positions with common volatility $\sigma$ and pairwise correlation $\rho$. Then $x^\top\Sigma x = x^2\sigma^2\big(n + n(n-1)\rho\big)$ and

$$
\frac{\text{IM}_{\text{port}}}{\sum_i \text{IM}_i} = \frac{\sigma\,x\sqrt{n + n(n-1)\rho}}{n\,\sigma\,x} = \sqrt{\frac{1+(n-1)\rho}{n}}.
$$

The inverse square of this ratio is $n/(1+(n-1)\rho)$, the effective breadth of Law 2 (§28.2). The CCP charges you for the number of independent bets you actually hold, which makes it the only counterparty in the building that has read Chapter 28. With $n = 100$ and $\rho = 0.3$ the ratio is $\sqrt{30.7/100} = 0.554$, so netting saves 45% of gross margin. A long-index, short-constituents book nets almost everything, which is why §22.6.1 finds clearing cheapest for dealers who hold the index *and* its single names at one CCP.

**The jump.** A volatility-scaled IM sees spreads, not defaults. A protection seller on one name can lose $N(1-R)$ overnight, which no $\sqrt{H}$ scaling of spread volatility captures. CCPs therefore add a jump-to-default charge on net sold protection, roughly $N_i\,(1 - R^{\text{stress}})$ less the position's mark, on the largest exposures, and size the default fund to survive the default of the two members to which they are most exposed (the "Cover 2" standard of the CPMI–IOSCO *Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures*, 2012, for systemically important CCPs). The jump is charged once, in its own line (Law 6). Netting it away against spread hedges is how a margin model fails on the morning it is needed.

**Table D.2. The CCP default waterfall (generic order; each CCP's rulebook governs).**

| Layer | Whose money | Note |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | Defaulter's initial margin | Sized to cover $H$ days at high confidence |
| 2 | Defaulter's default-fund contribution | |
| 3 | CCP's own capital ("skin in the game") | Small by design |
| 4 | Surviving members' default-fund contributions | Mutualized loss: your money, their default |
| 5 | Assessments on surviving members | Usually capped |
| 6 | Recovery tools (VM gains haircutting, tear-up) | The layer nobody wants to test |

**Table D.3. What is cleared, where, and how it is margined (approx.; check each CCP's current methodology).**

| Product | Clearing status | Main venues | IM | VM |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| CDX.NA.IG/HY, iTraxx Main/Crossover (standard tenors) | Mandatory for US persons since 2013 (CFTC, §22.6) | ICE Clear Credit; LCH CDSClear | Spread scenarios plus jump-to-default and liquidity add-ons; multi-day $H$ | Daily, cash |
| Single-name CDS | Voluntary (SEC security-based swaps; no mandate); dealer-to-dealer largely cleared | ICE Clear Credit; LCH CDSClear | As above; portfolio-margined against the indices | Daily, cash |
| Uncleared CDS, iBoxx total return swaps, bespokes | Bilateral under ISDA Master and CSA | None | Uncleared-margin rules for in-scope firms: ISDA SIMM, 10-day $H$, €50mm threshold; final phase from 2022-09-01 for groups above €8bn notional | Daily since 2017-03-01 for in-scope pairs |
